raw_title: Denza D9 vs MG M9 : Specs Comparison
title: Denza D9 vs MG M9 : Specs Comparison
raw_summary: GaadiWaadi - The Denza D9 brings a bigger battery and considerably more power, while the MG M9 counters with a longer wheelbase, an indulgent second row and a lower starting price The luxury electric MPV space in India has become a little more interesting with the arrival of the Denza D9. Priced at Rs 90 lakh, the BYD-owned luxury brand’s first Indian offering takes on the MG M9, which has already established itself as an option for buyers looking beyond conventional luxury SUVs. On paper, both have plenty going for them. They offer three rows of seating, powered sliding doors, elaborate second-row captain seats and a long list of comfort features. However, the differences become more apparent when you look at their battery packs, performance, dimensions and cabin equipment. Denza D9 vs MG M9: Specifications compared Specification Denza D9 MG M9 Ex-showroom price Rs 90 lakh Rs 79.94 lakh onwards Battery capacity 115.07 kWh 90 kWh Battery chemistry LFP (BYD Blade Battery) NMC Motor configuration Single motor Single motor Maximum power 462 hp 245 PS Maximum torque 365 Nm 350 Nm Drive type Front-wheel drive Front-wheel drive Claimed range 730 km (NEDC) 548 km (ARAI) 0-100 km/h 8.5 seconds Not officially specified AC charging 11 kW 11 kW DC charging Up to 1,500 kW Up to 160 kW Seating capacity 7 7 Seating layout 2+2+3 2+2+3 The D9 has a clear advantage in battery capacity and outright performance. Its 115.07 kWh Blade Battery is substantially larger than the 90 kWh pack in the M9. The front-mounted motor produces 462 hp and 365 Nm, compared with the M9’s 245 PS and 350 Nm. Range figures also favour the Denza on paper, with a claimed 730 km against the MG’s 548 km. There is an important distinction, though: the D9’s figure is based on the NEDC cycle, while the M9’s is ARAI-certified. These figures are not directly comparable, and actual driving range will depend on conditions and driving style. Charging is another interesting difference. Both support 11 kW AC charging, but the D9 advertises a particularly ambitious 10-97 per cent DC charging time of nine minutes, using compatible ultra-high-power charging infrastructure. Its quoted maximum charging power is 1,500 kW. The MG M9 supports up to 160 kW DC charging, with a claimed 30-80 per cent charge taking around 30 minutes. Dimensions Dimensions Denza D9 MG M9 Length 5,250 mm 5,270 mm Width 1,960 mm 2,000 mm Height 1,900 mm 1,840 mm Wheelbase 3,110 mm 3,200 mm Seating capacity 7 7 The MG M9 is marginally longer and noticeably wider, while its 3,200 mm wheelbase is 90 mm longer than that of the D9. This should give it an advantage in cabin packaging, particularly for rear passengers. The Denza, on the other hand, is taller. Both have large, upright MPV proportions and powered sliding doors, making access to the second and third rows easier. Cabin and comfort features This is where both MPVs make a strong case for themselves. The D9 gets Nappa leather upholstery across all three rows, with electrically adjustable front and second-row seats. The second-row captain seats get ventilation, heating, massage, memory and powered ottomans. The third row also gets four-way electric adjustment. The MG M9 takes a slightly different approach to rear-seat luxury. Its Presidential captain seats offer 16-way electric adjustment, massage, heating, ventilation and powered ottomans. They also get a lateral inward-glide function, allowing occupants to move the seats towards the centre of the cabin. Feature Denza D9 MG M9 Front touchscreen 15.6-inch 12.3-inch Digital instrument cluster 10.25-inch 7-inch Second-row seats Powered captain seats 16-way Presidential seats Seat ventilation Yes Yes Seat heating Yes Yes Massage function Yes Yes Powered ottomans Yes Yes Rear-seat controls Touchscreens integrated into armrests Dedicated touchscreen controls Sunroof Dual-sunroof setup Panoramic sunroof Climate control Three-zone Three-zone Audio system 16-speaker Devialet 13-speaker JBL Refrigerator Yes Not listed Wireless charging Four 50W positions Wireless charger Powered sliding doors Yes Yes Powered tailgate Yes Yes The D9 gets a larger infotainment touchscreen and instrument display, along with a 16-speaker Devialet sound system. Its party trick is the refrigerator integrated into the centre armrest, which can cool or warm items. There are also individual touchscreens in the second-row armrests to control seat functions. The M9 has a 13-speaker JBL audio system and offers a particularly well-equipped second row. Its Presidential seats are a major part of the experience, especially for buyers who expect to spend most of their time being driven around. It also gets rear entertainment screen compatibility and a panoramic sunroof. Safety and driver assistance Safety feature Denza D9 MG M9 Airbags 9 7 ADAS Level 2 Level 2 360-degree camera Yes Yes Blind-spot monitoring Yes Yes Electronic stability control Yes Yes Tyre pressure monitoring Yes Yes Euro NCAP rating Not listed 5 stars The Denza gets nine airbags, compared with seven in the MG. Both offer Level 2 ADAS and a 360-degree camera, along with the expected electronic safety systems. The MG M9 also has a five-star Euro NCAP rating, giving buyers an independently assessed safety result to consider. A directly comparable crash-test rating for the D9 is not listed here. Price and verdict The MG M9 starts at Rs 79.94 lakh (ex-showroom) for the Presidential Limo, while the limited-run Couture Edition is priced at Rs 84.94 lakh. The Denza D9 is available in a single, fully loaded configuration at Rs 90 lakh. That puts a little over Rs 10 lakh between the entry-level versions. MG also offers a Battery-as-a-Service option, with the M9 priced at Rs 69.99 lakh plus a battery usage charge of Rs 8 per kilometre. This changes the initial purchase outlay, although the running cost needs to be considered over the ownership period. The rest of the SUV looks familiar. The circular headlamps, vertical grille slots and chunky front bumper carry over on the unit pictured. The side view shows the five-door body, wide wheel-arch cladding and side steps. The wheels are the most visible change on this unit, while the more significant update is underneath.

The latest footage includes close-ups of the damper and coil spring assemblies. These add to the underbody views from the October sighting, which indicated that Mahindra was bringing its DaVinci suspension to the Roxx after introducing it on the Thar OG.

The current Thar Roxx already uses frequency-dependent damping. The DaVinci update is expected to build on that with revised internal damper valving, aimed at improving bump absorption and body control. For a five-door SUV that doubles as a family car, the difference would be most relevant on broken roads and stretches with repeated bumps, where passengers can feel how quickly the body settles after an impact. How much the ride improves will depend on the Roxx-specific tuning.

The dealership sighting suggests Mahindra is preparing to roll out the update. So far, the images show one unit outside a showroom. The launch date, variant-wise availability and any price revision are still awaited. It will also be worth seeing whether Mahindra introduces the suspension and wheel changes together across eligible trims or offers them on different variants.

The Thar Roxx is expected to continue with its existing 2.0-litre turbo-petrol and 2.2-litre diesel engines. The current range offers six-speed manual and torque-converter automatic gearboxes. Rear-wheel drive is available with both engines, while four-wheel drive is exclusive to the diesel. Equipment on higher variants currently includes a panoramic sunroof, ventilated front seats, a 360-degree camera and Level 2 ADAS.

For buyers already considering a Thar Roxx, the main detail to watch is which trims get the DaVinci dampers. The new alloys are easy to spot at a showroom. The suspension update will be easier to judge on a test drive over the sort of uneven roads the Roxx encounters in daily use.

title: Sonnen, SOLRITE, & ADAPT Energy, Integrating VPP Breakers to Turn Home Loads into Flexible Grid Assets
raw_summary: SOLRITE Unveils Next-Gen Virtual Power Plant Node with sonnen and ADAPT Energy, Integrating VPP Breakers to Turn Home Loads into Flexible Grid Assets ADAPT Energy’s control of VPP breakers will add dispatchable load flexibility to the SOLRITE sonnen VPP, while paving a simpler, faster, and lower-cost path to whole-home backup

article_paragraphs: SOLRITE Unveils Next-Gen Virtual Power Plant Node with sonnen and ADAPT Energy, Integrating VPP Breakers to Turn Home Loads into Flexible Grid Assets
ADAPT Energy’s control of VPP breakers will add dispatchable load flexibility to the SOLRITE sonnen VPP, while paving a simpler, faster, and lower-cost path to whole-home backup

SOLRITE, a company specializing in developing, financing, and owning Virtual Power Plant Agreement (VPA) projects, together with Sonnen, a leader in Virtual Power Plant energy storage technology, announced they will now digitally integrate VPP smart breakers, managed by ADAPT Energy, into the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. The integration marks the next evolution of sonnen and SOLRITE’s industry-leading partnership in VPP innovation, expanding beyond battery storage by transforming residential electrical loads into flexible, dispatchable grid assets for both the VPP and smart backup power applications.

Unlike traditional approaches to whole-home backup, often requiring hard-wired circuit relocation, including exclusive loads panels, the newly expanded VPP Node combines the sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to intelligently manage major household loads. This creates a more streamlined approach to whole-home backup while unlocking an entirely new source of flexibility for the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. With homeowner permission, the VPP smart breaker—controlled by ADAPT Energy—can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be flexible for both backup and grid participation.

“Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” said Regan George, CEO and Founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. Now, we’re going inside the home and unlocking another layer of flexibility that has been sitting there all along. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”

The integration addresses one of the longstanding challenges of whole-home backup: how to provide broad electrical coverage without having large household loads drain available battery capacity too quickly or cause the nano-grid to immediately fail after an off-grid transition due to excessive inrush current. With the newly expanded VPP smart breaker technology digitally integrated with the sonnen ecosystem, the system can intelligently shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns. This significantly reduces installation complexity and tedious inspections for installers, allowing crews to complete more jobs per week.

For homeowners, the system provides the convenience of a whole-home electrical configuration that intelligently manages the loads that have the greatest impact on backup duration. This work is all done in the background, meaning homeowners do not have to worry about resetting individual circuits during an outage. Instead, participating homes will see more value from their VPA program in the form of an enhanced backup power experience. Furthermore, at any time in the future, if a homeowner is interested in altering which of their VPP smart breaker-controlled loads are shed during an outage, the process to make such a change is quick and easy, requiring no electrical reconfiguration.

“This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” said Troy Morgan, President of PanTech Design , the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”

title: Hummer H1s May Be Nearly Indestructible, But Some Serious Flaws Live In That 'Nearly' Part
raw_summary: The Hummer brand officially launched in 1992 with the debut of its AM General High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle military-based civilian model. Much like the popularity of the Willys Jeep in post-WWII America, the H1 capitalized on rah-rah post-Gulf War nationalism and a personal endorsement from Arnold Schwarzenegger to find its place in the automotive zeitgeist. After being awarded its first military production contract in 1983, the big diesel-powered machine was well-proven by the time John Q. Public could place an order a decade later. If the HMMWV can be relied on by our fighting finest in the Muthanna Province, then surely it'll withstand the rigors of your suburban commute, right? Well, as it turns out, the answer is a cryptically Schrödinger-esque yes and no. When it comes to imposing four-wheeled machines, there's nothing quite as eye-catching and road-commanding as the original Hummer. Between 1992 and 1999, the vehicle was sold in small quantities by AM General's civilian division, but General Motors purchased the rights to market and distribute the Hummer brand for the new millennium. With just shy of 12,000 units sold across the truck's entire production run, these things are a bit thin on the ground, but they maintain a strong cultural significance today, and the appeal of a genuine mil-spec vehicle is hard to deny.

If the HMMWV can be relied on by our fighting finest in the Muthanna Province, then surely it'll withstand the rigors of your suburban commute, right? Well, as it turns out, the answer is a cryptically Schrödinger-esque yes and no.

When it comes to imposing four-wheeled machines, there's nothing quite as eye-catching and road-commanding as the original Hummer. Between 1992 and 1999, the vehicle was sold in small quantities by AM General's civilian division, but General Motors purchased the rights to market and distribute the Hummer brand for the new millennium. With just shy of 12,000 units sold across the truck's entire production run, these things are a bit thin on the ground, but they maintain a strong cultural significance today, and the appeal of a genuine mil-spec vehicle is hard to deny.

Because of its high profile and rarity, every variant of the H1 generally still commands a pretty penny, even two decades after production ended. A high-mileage early non-turbo diesel model might bring as low as $35,000, while a low-mileage 2006-only H1 Alpha runs into the low six-figure range. If you're going to be spending that much money to get yourself one of these rolling monuments of gender-affirming care, what trouble should you expect and look out for? Let's dig into it.

The first issue is that, simply due to their size and material density, they're really heavy. At around 7,500 pounds, you're moving a lot of metal around. Weight translates to atrocious fuel economy, like about 10 miles per gallon bad. Another downside: due to the military-based nature of these trucks, driver comfort is hardly a concern, and the noise, vibration, and harshness engineers were not really consulted in the design phase. According to a Hagerty review , the "engine sounds like a jackhammer inside the cockpit." Oh, and it doesn't have airbags.

On the plus side, a Hummer H1 is mostly indestructible, except for one major flaw. If you're a long-time reader of Jalopnik, you'll probably know where this is going, because over a decade ago our own Doug Demuro found out firsthand what breaks on the Hummer H1 . I'll let him explain it.

"Beginning in about 1996, every single Hummer was fitted with a 6.5-liter Detroit Diesel turbodiesel V8, which combined the 194 horsepower of a Toyota Camry with the 438 lb-ft of torque from an angry farm tractor.

Well, there was one little issue: every single one of these engines was manufactured with a casting flaw that resulted in a crack on the number eight cylinder. Fortunately, the fix was easy: you just replaced the engine.

But check this out: it affected every single Hummer manufactured from 1996 to 2000... Every single Hummer built from 1996 to 2000 has either had its engine fail due to the number eight cylinder issue, or will have its engine fail."

raw_title: Rocket Fuel: The Last Frontier For Natural Gas
title: Rocket Fuel: The Last Frontier For Natural Gas
raw_summary: Fossil fuels are slowly beginning to lose their grip on the global transportation sector, with one key omission: rocket fuel. The rocket fuel conundrum has earned an uptick in attention in recent years, now that rocket launches, once rare, are becoming as commonplace as rush hour traffic. The Elon Musk venture SpaceX, for example, is building new natural gas pipelines in order to produce its own methane-based propellant, needed to sustain the launch of many thousands of rockets in the coming years. Not all rocket fuel is methane-based, but that’s where some aerospace firms, including SpaceX, have landed in the pursuit of space domination. Methane is processed from natural gas, stripping away nitrogen and other impurities. Liquefied and mixed with liquid oxygen, it becomes a powerful propellant.

Not all rocket fuel is methane-based, but that’s where some aerospace firms, including SpaceX, have landed in the pursuit of space domination. Methane is processed from natural gas, stripping away nitrogen and other impurities. Liquefied and mixed with liquid oxygen, it becomes a powerful propellant.

With its future volume of launch operations in mind, SpaceX aims to exercise as much control as possible over its fuel supply. The company is investing in its own natural gas pipelines and on-site fuel production facilities to help ensure that the taps don’t run dry, though it still relies on the gas industry to find the stuff and bring it up from the ground.

SpaceX has already been sucking up a copious amount of natural gas for its existing operations in Texas and Florida. “SpaceX (SPCX) is emerging as one of the largest new customers for natural gas,” reported the oil and gas analytics firm East Daley in October.

“Unlike Falcon 9, which burns rocket-grade kerosene and liquid oxygen, Starship creates a direct link between launch activity and natural gas consumption. SPCX plans to process and liquefy pipeline gas into liquid methane to fuel the rockets,” East Daley elaborates.

As described by East Daley, the SpaceX subsidiary Coastal Connect Services is planning a 32.4-mile natural gas pipeline to hook up SpaceX operations in Cape Canaveral, Florida with existing infrastructure jointly owned by Kinder Morgan and Energy Transfer.

Meanwhile, at the company’s launch site and newly incorporated (as of 2025) City of Starbase in Cameron County, Texas, plans are in motion for SpaceX affiliate Lone Star Mineral Development to connect the new 8-mile “Starpipe” natural gas pipeline with another 145-mile pipeline currently being built by the firms WhiteWater, Enbridge, and MPLX. Starpipe is expected to begin shuttling natural gas into Starbase Texas early next year.

The two pipeline projects come alongside word that SpaceX has nailed down approvals for parts of a new $100 billion project that expands the company’s US footprint into another combination city-and-launch-site under the name of Starbase, Louisiana. The new city will presumably also require a reliable supply of natural gas for on-site rocket fuel production.

title: This Honda Civic Is The Direct Ancestor Of The OG Tesla Roadster
raw_summary: Tom Gage is the one-time CEO of a company you probably don't remember, called AC Propulsion. However, that firm was one of the progenitors of EVs and, by extension, Tesla. Gage is also the one-time owner of this 1994 Honda Civic. This past weekend he sold it, and we should explain why that's important. See, underneath its aged sheet metal, it wasn't a Civic at all, but more of a science experiment. It has no tailpipe because Gage's partner, AC Propulsion co-founder Alan Cocconi, gutted the little hatchback in 1994 to fill with lead-acid bricks and convert the Civic into a proof-of-concept electric car that led to the rise of Tesla. The Tesla link is that AC Propulsion used the Civic to try out systems that would later debut on the company's 1998 tzero electric Roadster. That car looked cooler, but had the same tech that powered the electric Honda. And it's that technology that Tesla eventually licensed in 2004 and that ended up featuring in the original Tesla Roadster in 2008.

Gage is also the one-time owner of this 1994 Honda Civic. This past weekend he sold it, and we should explain why that's important.
article_paragraphs: Tom Gage is the one-time CEO of a company you probably don't remember, called AC Propulsion. However, that firm was one of the progenitors of EVs and, by extension, Tesla. Gage is also the one-time owner of this 1994 Honda Civic. This past weekend he sold it, and we should explain why that's important.

See, underneath its aged sheet metal, it wasn't a Civic at all, but more of a science experiment. It has no tailpipe because Gage's partner, AC Propulsion co-founder Alan Cocconi, gutted the little hatchback in 1994 to fill with lead-acid bricks and convert the Civic into a proof-of-concept electric car that led to the rise of Tesla. The Tesla link is that AC Propulsion used the Civic to try out systems that would later debut on the company's 1998 tzero electric Roadster. That car looked cooler, but had the same tech that powered the electric Honda. And it's that technology that Tesla eventually licensed in 2004 and that ended up featuring in the original Tesla Roadster in 2008.

We interviewed Gage, who explained that it wasn't electric propulsion (at first) that attracted Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard to EVs — and, eventually, Elon Musk. It was actually its sexy shape, which was just a kit car called the Piontek Sportech. "I mean, that was exactly the reason we built the tzero in the first place," Gage explains. "EVs still had this golf cart image, and so even with lead-acid batteries, the tzero would be zero to 60 in the four-second range." This is funny because, actually, the Honda was just as fast. The tale of how AC Propulsion went from gutting Civics to making electric Scions and, eventually, helping spawn the iconic Tesla Roadster, is fascinating. It even includes a bit of spying, too.

Some of Cocconi's engineering that made it into this 1994 Honda Civic was way ahead of its time. For instance, Gage says Cocconi devised a module that could produce AC-to-DC (and vice-versa) power flow. "When you were driving, [it] could take the DC current from the battery and convert it to high-frequency AC to run the motor. And when you weren't driving, and you plugged it in, the same inverter components would convert the AC from the grid into DC to charge the battery."

Modern EVs have this capability, but even today, something Cocconi worked on isn't ubiquitous — feeding power from the EV back to your home or to the grid. AC Propulsion cars were eventually capable of that at up to 20 kilowatts, while the 2027 Ford Fathom will be able to do this without a wall inverter at 10 kW.

According to Gage, the Civic had the first iteration of the 200-horsepower system, which the firm called a power electronics unit because it was more than just the motor and inverter. It contained that, as well as the charger, and the ability to push out a 12-volt DC power supply, which the Civic (or any car) needs since all of its components run on 12 volts.

Even back in the 1990s, AC Propulsion was looking for solutions that still bedevil carmakers today. For instance, how do you get reasonable all-electric range and fight battery weight simultaneously? At first, because the company was working with lead-acid batteries, they were stuck with limited range, and those batteries were far heavier than later lithium cells. Gage says that with batteries aboard, the Civic exceeded the gross vehicle limit of what the chassis was designed for, with the batteries alone weighing 1,200 pounds.

Fixing this required fitting a trailer with a gas engine aboard to operate as a range-extending generator, which topped up the batteries while driving. This created a series hybrid rather than a parallel hybrid, and the difference is that series hybrids only run their gas motors as generators — the engines don't power the wheels. Hence, putting the motor on a trailer works just fine. "We had several generations," Gage laughed. "We had some kind of a Generac standard generator, which we modified in various ways, but the exhaust was really stinky and [it] didn't have that much power."

It’s a win for democracy when millions of citizens peacefully claim their right to a government of, by, and for the people.

Will the Trump administration acknowledge voters’ repudiation of its destructive agenda and work in cooperation with this new Congress? That remains to be seen, and I’m not holding my breath. But there’s no question that the shift in Congress has significant implications for the administration’s ability to continue to ram through its anti-science , authoritarian agenda—including on climate and clean energy issues.

Energy affordability concerns, opposition to proliferating data centers , and anger at corruption and extreme economic inequality were undoubtedly driving forces in how people voted. While not everyone explicitly named climate change as a top issue (although many did put it in their top three ), its fingerprints are all over the issues a majority of voters did name in polls.

If you care about addressing the high costs of electricity and gas, then you must reckon with the fact that this current fossil energy crisis, unleashed by the Trump administration’s war against Iran, is an extreme manifestation of the risks of fossil fuel dependence. The benefits of a transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy—renewable energy that the Trump administration has relentlessly attacked, further driving up costs for consumers—are tremendous. If you are deeply concerned about the rapid, unregulated build-out of data centers, you know that it comes with huge risks for communities related to climate, water, pollution, health, and electricity cost burdens. And it’s so clear that the Trump administration’s corruption, lies about climate science , and massive giveaways to fossil fuel polluters are leaving us all bearing the high costs of climate damages while large corporations and the president’s inner circle are raking in enormous profits .

Here’s another reality: regardless of politics, climate change is here, and science shows it’s rapidly worsening with the world’s imminent overshoot of 1.5°C of global warming. Communities are already experiencing deadly and costly climate impacts, including extreme heatwaves, catastrophic wildfires, record-breaking flooding, drought, accelerating sea level rise, intense ocean heat, irreversible loss of glaciers and ice sheets, stresses to critical ecosystems and more. These impacts are showing up in people’s daily lives—harming their health, destroying homes, livelihoods, and critical infrastructure, raising insurance premiums, hammering businesses, stressing water supplies, and threatening food security and affordability.

Climate change and clean energy are pocketbook issues. They are a lot more than that, of course. And climate change does not care if you live in a red state or a blue state. (One can ask if that is that even a relevant frame after an election that scrambled all conventional wisdom about “red” and “blue” dichotomies.)

Importantly, we will soon have a Congress where a majority accepts the scientific evidence on climate change. (Yes, I also wish we could take that for granted in 2026, but not in US politics, sadly.) That’s an important start and means we can advocate for policymakers to legislate based on the facts, instead of being stuck fighting disinformation and lies.
Here’s what this seismic “change election” could mean for action on climate change, some cautions about what likely won’t change right away, and what we’ll have to keep fighting for.

raw_title: The Crucial Difference Between Flock Cameras And Plate Readers In Other Countries
title: The Crucial Difference Between Flock Cameras And Plate Readers In Other Countries
raw_summary: Stories about Flock cameras and other stalkerish automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) have been a mainstay of American news for the last year or two, and horror stories involving this questionable technology are everywhere. From police using ALPRs to stalk citizens to AI-powered ALPRs flagging innocent auto journalists for stealing vehicles , there's no shortage of evidence that ALPRs are making the world worse. A lot of such stories you see in the news and even here on Jalopnik are about misuse of and issues with ALPRs specifically in the United States, though. While there's certainly some bias toward American news on publications based in the States, it still does raise the question: Are there Flock cameras or equivalents in other countries? And if so, do they cause the same volume of issues? The answer is an interesting one. First, yes, ALPRs do exist outside of the United States, though the technology is often called automatic number plate recognition, or ANPR, due to regional differences in how license plates are referred to. Nearly 100 countries use this technology to track automobile movement and other data. However, Flock cameras themselves aren't nearly as prevalent outside the United States. In fact, the big difference between the implementation of license plate recognition technology in the U.S. and abroad is in who owns it and how the data collected is managed.

article_paragraphs: Stories about Flock cameras and other stalkerish automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) have been a mainstay of American news for the last year or two, and horror stories involving this questionable technology are everywhere. From police using ALPRs to stalk citizens to AI-powered ALPRs flagging innocent auto journalists for stealing vehicles , there's no shortage of evidence that ALPRs are making the world worse. A lot of such stories you see in the news and even here on Jalopnik are about misuse of and issues with ALPRs specifically in the United States, though. While there's certainly some bias toward American news on publications based in the States, it still does raise the question: Are there Flock cameras or equivalents in other countries? And if so, do they cause the same volume of issues?

The answer is an interesting one. First, yes, ALPRs do exist outside of the United States, though the technology is often called automatic number plate recognition, or ANPR, due to regional differences in how license plates are referred to. Nearly 100 countries use this technology to track automobile movement and other data. However, Flock cameras themselves aren't nearly as prevalent outside the United States. In fact, the big difference between the implementation of license plate recognition technology in the U.S. and abroad is in who owns it and how the data collected is managed.

See, Flock Safety and Axon, two of the biggest promulgators of ALPR tech in the States, are privately operated companies that contract their services out to the state via entities like police departments and city councils. In other countries, and European countries in particular, ALPRs are typically owned, deployed, and operated by the state itself, rather than subcontracted through private companies. This distinction might just make all the difference.

If you're skeptical that a state-owned surveillance network is different than a privately owned, state-sponsored surveillance, well, you know, that's fair. But there are indeed some notable differences between how this technology is treated in the U.S. and how it's used abroad.

The rest of the world is certainly no stranger to surveillance. For example, the UK has a massive network of CCTV cameras that leave urban areas like London heavily monitored at all times, and they're now employing AI to level up their surveillance efforts, too. AI-powered surveillance is also rapidly ramping up in China, Brazil, and Australia.

Whether these networks are installed and operated by governments or private entities, the fact is that there's room for abuse by those with access to the data. However, in some other locations, it's easier for governments to regulate and oversee how the data is used. For example, European ALPR data is protected by the region's General Data Protection Regulation, which is way more than we have here in the ALPR Wild West.

In the U.S., Flock data from one municipality can be accessed by basically anyone in other areas with a Flock contract, and hackers who pulled a Flock camera apart showed that it's pretty easy to get the stored data even without a contract. Some police officers have even been caught accessing Flock data after leaving the force, according to the Washington Post . When this happens, finding accountability can be hard. ALPRs owned and run by the state directly at least have clear channels for voicing dissent, though it may also be true that they're more entrenched and harder to remove.

Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, has reportedly signed a $3.4 billion contract to buy gas-fired engines (power plants) from OnePWR Solutions, a Texas-based energy company. These gas power plants would be able to provide Anthropic’s AI data centers with an enormous amount of off-grid electricity — with the real cost being an enormous amount of air pollution and global warming emissions.
If you thought Anthropic was supposed to be “the good guy” in the AI industry, perhaps think again.

The Financial Times , which broke the news on this, says that this is the “largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab.” It’s this line from Futurism that really sums up my feelings: “It isn’t just symptomatic of a desperate race to secure the necessary utilities: it’s also one of the clearest signs yet that the AI industry has turned its back on the growing climate crisis in favor of pollution-spewing gas generators it’s installing across the globe.” Indeed. It’s one thing to be racing to be a leader in this field, but to turn to polluting, climate-destroying gas power plants instead of solar and wind power, that’s absolutely disappointing and — frankly — morally disgusting.
For the heck of it, to see what this company’s AI bot thought about the power choice it made, I decided to ask Claude “Are gas power plants harmful to our climate?” The response was as follows:
“Yes, though they’re less harmful than coal and more harmful than most alternatives.

“Bottom line: Gas is a cleaner fossil fuel, not a clean one. Its climate impact is best judged by what it replaces (coal vs. renewables) and by how tightly methane leaks are controlled. Carbon capture could reduce plant emissions, but it’s still costly and not widely deployed.”

So, yeah, when you’re choosing to buy $3.4 billion worth of gas power plants instead of renewable energy power plants, that is without a doubt going to be a horrible decision for our climate. I’m sure if I asked Claude about the risk humans race from climate change, the answer would not be uplifting. But I’m not going to go there. Instead, I’ll turn back to Futurism for this summary: “Researchers have found that the effects of AI on the environment are nothing short of devastating . And the prognosis for the future is grim. Last month, environmental nonprofit Sierra Club estimated that upcoming AI data centers could release 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030, wiping out nearly 15 years worth of greenhouse gas reduction efforts.”

title: What A Road Sign With A Black 'Y' Means (And Other Letters, Too)
raw_summary: We have covered all manner of weird road signs on Jalopnik before, including some seriously goofy ones . While oddities from around the globe are fun to explore and explain, it is a little more relevant to touch on road signs that crop up on U.S. soil. Some of these will no doubt be familiar, but others may not, so there is good reason to delve into them and provide a quick explainer. The black "Y" sign was the one that initially piqued our interest, which, by the way, highlights that a Y-shaped intersection is to be found up ahead. That led us to look at other weird letter- and symbol-focused road signs drivers may come across. The obvious candidates are "P" for parking areas and "H" that marks hospitals, which are universally understood, but throughout this article, we will also explore what those weird "T" or upturned "U" signs mean, in addition to winding "S" and plus-symbol signs. That includes where drivers are most likely to find them and how best to react when they do. Listed in no particular order, here are our picks of eight letter- or symbol-focused road signs that we thought are worth exploring in a bit more detail.

That led us to look at other weird letter- and symbol-focused road signs drivers may come across.

The obvious candidates are "P" for parking areas and "H" that marks hospitals, which are universally understood, but throughout this article, we will also explore what those weird "T" or upturned "U" signs mean, in addition to winding "S" and plus-symbol signs. That includes where drivers are most likely to find them and how best to react when they do. Listed in no particular order, here are our picks of eight letter- or symbol-focused road signs that we thought are worth exploring in a bit more detail.

As already explained briefly above, a sign that depicts a capitalized "Y" is there to let drivers know of a Y-shaped three-way intersection or a forked road ahead. The sign will typically be a diamond shape with a yellow background, which means it's a simple warning sign alerting drivers that the road splits. The choices of where to go are obvious — either left or right — but what might be less obvious is how the right of way is determined in a three-way intersection that isn't controlled by any other signs.

The general rule is that drivers must yield to the car on the right. Then there's always the first-to-arrive rule, which works as you would intend — the first to arrive at the split goes first. Of course, some drivers will assume right of way when it is not deserved, or perhaps they just do not see the other car(s). In such instances, it's best to yield to the other vehicle even if you believe you should have the right of way to ensure everyone gets past the intersection without incident.

When a road splits like this, it pays to be especially cautious. Drivers may attempt to dart from one lane to the next when correcting a last-minute wrong decision, plus motorbikes or cyclists could be hiding in your blind spots, so try to ensure you have sufficient space around you if possible. The NHTSA highlights that roughly one third of all traffic fatalities occur at signposted intersections, so doubling down on cautiousness here is never a bad idea, no matter how simple it may first appear.

Surprise surprise, the letter "T" on a road sign warns of a T-shaped intersection — we would hope that you managed to work that one out. The road you are traveling on is about to end and merge with another. Once again, this is a classic warning sign finished in a yellow and black colorway, on a diamond-shaped sign that lets drivers know something's coming up and they will have to act accordingly.

In this instance, drivers must yield to traffic on the intersecting road — they don't have the right of way here — before heading either left or right. There will usually be a stop or yield sign prior to the intersection itself, and to avoid any frustrating bumps with other drivers making late decisions, it's best to get into the required lane early rather than last-minute. Thankfully, of the deadliest intersections on U.S. roads , not many are T-shaped, but the same rules as above apply here. Give yourself space, keep an eye on your blind spots, and don't rush. Oh, and don't forget to use your turn signals either, even if you are in a dedicated turn lane .

Again, we won't be handing out prizes to anyone who is able to correctly guess this one. A cross or "plus" symbol indicates that a crossroad is coming up, and just like the other aforementioned sign, this too will be depicted on a black and yellow diamond-shaped warning sign. Here, traffic can and likely will be coming from all directions, so it's imperative to take the time that's needed and approach it with care. Be aware that drivers on the opposite leg might try to cross ahead of you as you pull out, and be sure to check traffic from both left and right directions. As always, make sure to follow the instructions depicted on any regulatory signs posted in your direction, as these might detail give-way instructions.

raw_title: Every Car Brand That's Made A V10-Powered Sedan
title: Every Car Brand That's Made A V10-Powered Sedan
raw_summary: With downsizing being a priority today, thanks chiefly to ever-stricter emissions regulations, a good number of supercars are being sold with six-cylinder engines. In fact, you could even argue that some four-cylinder cars could qualify as supercars today. However, less than a decade earlier, we had a trio of V10-powered sedans sitting in mainstream automaker showrooms — crazy, yet that was the reality of the '00s super-sedan market. BMW dropped a 5.0-liter V10 mill into an otherwise fairly regular-looking 5 Series, Audi furnished its S- and RS-badged sedans with a 5.2-liter lump, and Volkswagen went so far as to develop a diesel-powered V10 for its Bentley-based luxobarge that hardly anyone even remembers existed. This article shines a light on those fascinating 10-cylinder sedans, zeroing in on the prices, performance specs, and general absurdity each brought to the table. We'll also take a look at how much each example commands today, and what litany of issues typically drain the wallet of anyone foolish enough to take one on. While those models are listed below in chronological order of release, we've also included a brief look at a pair of show-stopping V10-powered sedan concepts that sadly never saw the light of day. One was silenced by a shift in direction, while another found itself permanently postponed by the hands of the '08 financial crisis.

While those models are listed below in chronological order of release, we've also included a brief look at a pair of show-stopping V10-powered sedan concepts that sadly never saw the light of day. One was silenced by a shift in direction, while another found itself permanently postponed by the hands of the '08 financial crisis.

The Volkswagen Phaeton was the first 10-cylinder sedan to break onto the market. It arrived in 2003, designed to elevate Volkswagen's position in the car industry, and Ferdinand Piëch and his team equipped it with all the vital tools to do so. Air suspension, immensely comfortable leather seats, a ridiculously complex A/C system , and a whole host of cool engine options.

The base model came with Volkswagen's weird VR6 , which sounds ace and delivers a respectable punch of power — as does the optional 4.2-liter V8. A 3.0-liter direct-injection turbodiesel (TDI) was available in other markets, but for the big spenders, Volkswagen offered both a 6.0-liter W12 and a 4.9-liter V10 TDI. The latter produced 313 horsepower alongside 553 pound-feet of torque – ample for a German luxury sedan at the time.

It wasn't an option that made it to the U.S. market. Instead, Americans received the V8 and W12. Across the pond in the U.K., though, the V10 Phaeton went on sale in early 2003 with a sticker of £57,840, or the equivalent of $95,574 back then. Adjusted for inflation, that comes out to about $175,000 today. Depreciation has really played its part with this forgotten flagship, though, and as a result, prices rarely top £10,000 ($13,480) today. Meanwhile, its W12-powered counterparts regularly trade hands for around $15,000 to $20,000 in the U.S., depending on mileage.

As for what to watch out for, the consensus is just about everything. There was little room in the engine bay, so owners detail that some jobs — like turbocharger replacement — are an engine-out ordeal. That makes work both labor-intensive and not DIY-friendly, and big bills make what is essentially a fancy Passat quite difficult to justify.

It was the E60-generation M5 that next appeared on the 10-cylinder sedan scene, debuting as a 2005 model year. Unlike the Phaeton, which was sold as a comfort-first luxury car, the E60 M5 was first and foremost a performance car. It famously takes power from the naturally aspirated S85 5.0-liter V10, which delivers 500 hp alongside 384 lb-ft of torque. A high compression ratio of 12:1 ensured the M5 meets its 100-hp-per-liter target, and it revs all the way to 8,250 rpm, too. The brilliance of this design was rewarded with the coveted International Engine of the Year Award in both '05 and '06, and it's an engine that still attracts much enthusiast attention 20-plus years later.

When new, buyers would have had to fork out $84,895 for one of these V10-powered super-sedans, and while they have indeed depreciated quite heavily over the last two decades, prices are once again on the move. Classic.com shows $25,555 as the average price paid for SMG-equipped examples, while six-speed manual cars command a significant premium at $45,127. That premium comes down to collectors cherishing the stick-shift involvement, but also ostensibly to the fact that SMG transmissions are so troublesome and expensive to repair — hydraulic pump failures are regular and can easily set owners back thousands of dollars to correct. Aside from SMG woes, the V10 itself is particularly trouble-prone, with its oil pump, throttle body actuators, and rod bearings being known weak spots.

title: Chinese Competition May Cause EV Tariff Delays In The EU And UK
raw_summary: A proposed 10% levy on electric vehicles that don't have locally sourced battery materials may be postponed by the European Union and the UK. It's because supply chains haven't been able to keep up with the planned rollout, with most UK- and EU-manufactured EVs still reliant on Asian-sourced materials for crucial battery components. The plans, which were drawn up during 2021's finalized Brexit negotiations, are different from the EU's postponed plans to go EV-only from 2035 . These relate to the origin of EV components, and were supposed to roll out on January 1, 2027, with tough requirements for any EV traded between the UK and EU that did not feature battery packs assembled locally.

article_paragraphs: A proposed 10% levy on electric vehicles that don't have locally sourced battery materials may be postponed by the European Union and the UK. It's because supply chains haven't been able to keep up with the planned rollout, with most UK- and EU-manufactured EVs still reliant on Asian-sourced materials for crucial battery components.

The plans, which were drawn up during 2021's finalized Brexit negotiations, are different from the EU's postponed plans to go EV-only from 2035 . These relate to the origin of EV components, and were supposed to roll out on January 1, 2027, with tough requirements for any EV traded between the UK and EU that did not feature battery packs assembled locally.

The Financial Times reports that ACEA, a group that represents EU automakers, claims that the vast majority of the 520,000 EV passenger vehicles — some 82% — that are being projected for sale during 2027 would be subject to the levy. The UK is the largest buyer of EU-manufactured vehicles, with 30% of them sold across the channel. Similarly, the UK's biggest export market for EVs is the EU, with the two trading some €80 billion ($88 billion) each year.

The ACEA argues that if the levy came into effect, UK- and EU-made EVs would no longer be competitive with rivals from China — themselves subject to import limitations — as the EU attempts to reduce its trade deficit. There's an element of irony there though, as most battery packs and chemicals used in these vehicles originate in Asia, with many imported from China. ACEA has proposed postponing the requirements until 2030, and pushing the additional requirement for European-made battery cathode material to 2032.

While European carmakers are pushing for the delay, the flip side of the coin includes European companies that have already invested in large-scale battery manufacturing facilities, as well as the EU chemicals industry. According to the report, while a delay to the 10% levy being implemented is likely, it's unclear as to how long it will be staved off. An unquoted UK official said that serious negotiations will likely begin after an EU-UK summit, which is scheduled for November 20, 2026.

raw_title: SpaceX's Rivals Are Already Filling The Void Left By Falcon 9
title: SpaceX's Rivals Are Already Filling The Void Left By Falcon 9
raw_summary: The future of American access to space is in doubt for the first time in decades. That very uncertainty is already starting to show itself as an opportunity for the companies positioned to seize it. In the last few weeks, the Pentagon has handed out two separate $150 million loans to rocket companies Stoke Space and Rocket Lab, investments meant to build out their launch infrastructure and manufacturing capabilities. That ought to help get them to a place where they can reliably launch military assets into space, but critically, it also helps them attract and deliver on commercial contracts, too. Business is booming, and a lot more is expected to come the way of these two and many other rocket companies in the next few years. The main reason: SpaceX, the dominant force in the entire sector, is giving that business away. Elon Musk's rocket enterprise has expanded a lot lately, getting into everything from AI infrastructure to natural gas mining . Its future mainly depends on the in-development Starship rocket, however. The largest and most powerful rocket ever built, it is supposedly taking astronauts to the Moon and is the only rocket that can deploy Starlink's newest V3 satellites. SpaceX really, really needs Starship to work. So it's acting as if it will work, which means the company has already stopped taking reservations for flights on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket . While it appears that the military and NASA may get a few extra years to use that rocket , Musk has made it clear he intends to wind down the Falcon 9 sooner rather than later.

That very uncertainty is already starting to show itself as an opportunity for the companies positioned to seize it. In the last few weeks, the Pentagon has handed out two separate $150 million loans to rocket companies Stoke Space and Rocket Lab, investments meant to build out their launch infrastructure and manufacturing capabilities. That ought to help get them to a place where they can reliably launch military assets into space, but critically, it also helps them attract and deliver on commercial contracts, too. Business is booming, and a lot more is expected to come the way of these two and many other rocket companies in the next few years. The main reason: SpaceX, the dominant force in the entire sector, is giving that business away.

Elon Musk's rocket enterprise has expanded a lot lately, getting into everything from AI infrastructure to natural gas mining . Its future mainly depends on the in-development Starship rocket, however. The largest and most powerful rocket ever built, it is supposedly taking astronauts to the Moon and is the only rocket that can deploy Starlink's newest V3 satellites. SpaceX really, really needs Starship to work. So it's acting as if it will work, which means the company has already stopped taking reservations for flights on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket . While it appears that the military and NASA may get a few extra years to use that rocket , Musk has made it clear he intends to wind down the Falcon 9 sooner rather than later.

The question is, what happens if Starship isn't ready in the next few years? Even if it is, what if it's so busy launching Starlink satellites that it won't take other customers? Plus, as a larger rocket, Starship will likely be more expensive to commission than other rockets. Where does the rest of the space ecosystem, including the military, go once the Falcon 9 is gone?

The Pentagon sees the coming crunch in launch capacity and is moving now to mitigate it. It wants more companies capable of delivering its payloads to orbit to reduce its dependence on one provider and, really, one particular business leader. That's why its Office of Strategic Capital, the military's investment arm established in 2022, is pouring resources into SpaceX's smaller rivals right now. For Stoke Space, this money is intended to help it build out a new launchpad at the Space Force base in Cape Canaveral , where its in-development Nova Block 2 rocket will operate. For Rocket Lab, the money will help it upgrade its factories and expand its drone boat fleet for the recovery of returning rockets.

It's not a coincidence that Stoke's Nova Block 2 and Rocket Lab's in-development Neutron rocket are more or less competitors to the departing Falcon 9, not Starship. Though they are a bit smaller, capable of 15 and 13 metric-ton payloads respectively compared to the Falcon 9's 23, that still puts them in position to scoop up business for medium-sized missions. For a lot of satellite and other space companies, that's all they need, so it's a better fit for them than a more expensive Starship launch. And that's assuming Starship would even take reservations for launches beyond its Starlink needs.

Still, that word "in-development" keeps cropping up, which is its own cause for concern. All of these rockets need to actually prove they can launch and recover reliably, or there's no business at all. The Neutron rocket already delayed its debut to 2027; the Nova Block 2 isn't scheduled to start flying until 2029. It really puts into perspective how far ahead of its time the Falcon 9 was. Of course, there are other competitors knocking at the door, most notably Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin and its New Glenn rocket . What will determine the next decade of the space industry is how many of these rockets come online when and how successfully.

As the Russo-Ukrainian War has proven, space is a critical component of modern warfare; in multiple instances , Ukraine's sudden disconnection from Starlink ( reportedly at Musk's behest ) directly impacted its ability to conduct strike operations. Those instances also prove the fragility of depending on one company. So these investments are meant to diversify the Pentagon's corporate partners in this domain, giving it several ways to reach and, in the future, utilize space. Redundancy is going to be key to military space endeavors in the event of a war with a near-peer adversary.

However, it's worth noting that investments in launch infrastructure and manufacturing also set up these companies for success in their launches for commercial clients, which in turn nurtures the whole space industry. As a primary strategic concern for the 21 st century, the American government is essentially subsidizing the growth of the entire space sector. The more companies are active here, the more innovations and technologies are created. Those then become the engines of both economic and military might. As ever with the military-industrial complex, it feeds on itself.

raw_title: 9 Cheaper Alternatives To The Toyota Land Cruiser
title: 9 Cheaper Alternatives To The Toyota Land Cruiser
raw_summary: The Toyota Land Cruiser is synonymous with toughness and reliability. It is a reputation it has been earning for more than 70 years. Toyota first used the Land Cruiser name in 1954 to describe the small all-wheel-drive truck developed for the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force. Over the decades, the Land Cruiser has grown more luxurious but never abandoned its rugged roots. The current 250-series Land Cruiser sold in the U.S. is based on the smaller Prado model sold in other countries. It is not only physically smaller than the 200-series it replaced, but it also has a much lower price tag as well. In 2021, the 200-series Land Cruiser started at a little more than $87,000 with delivery, processing, and handling fees. Today, a new Land Cruiser 1958 starts at $59,775, all fees included. That is a significant price cut for what is still a very capable body-on-frame SUV.

In 2021, the 200-series Land Cruiser started at a little more than $87,000 with delivery, processing, and handling fees. Today, a new Land Cruiser 1958 starts at $59,775, all fees included. That is a significant price cut for what is still a very capable body-on-frame SUV.

The 2027 Land Cruiser is powered by a hybrid 2.4-liter turbocharged i-Force Max powertrain that produces a combined 326 horsepower and 465 pound-feet of torque. Meanwhile, standard full-time four-wheel drive with a two-speed transfer case and crawl control ensures it will get the entire family to the campsite — or the local Whole Foods.

For this list, we wanted to present buyers with a diverse set of alternatives that deliver many of the Land Cruiser's main strengths at a significantly lower price. These include models that prioritize rugged off-road ability, while others focus a bit more on practicality, comfort, and even a dose of luxury. There is something for everyone in this list, and every one of them will save you serious money. Without further ado, here are nine of those alternatives ranked from the most to the least expensive. All the MSRPs cited in this article include handling and destination fees.

We start the list by looking in Toyota's own backyard. Starting at $55,085, the Toyota 4Runner TRD Off-Road i-Force Max is the most expensive Land Cruiser alternative on our list, but it is still several thousand less than the base Land Cruiser. Although Toyota believes they appeal to different buyers , the 4Runner TRD Off-Road i-Force Max and the Land Cruiser share the exact same powertrain. The similarities continue with the same body-on-frame TNGA-F platform, two-speed transfer case, "crawl control," and more. However, the 4Runner actually holds the edge in ground clearance (9.1 inches versus 8.1 inches, respectively). In an off-road battle, there isn't going to be much in it between them.

The Land Cruiser has the edge in interior space, however. You get more head, shoulder, hip, and leg room compared to the 4Runner. The Land Cruiser also offers 46.2 cubic feet of cargo space behind the second row of seats compared to 42.6 for the 4Runner TRD Off-Road i-FORCE MAX. Although all 4Runner models do have that beloved power rear window.

For most buyers, the decision will likely come down to exterior styling and space requirements. The two rigs are very similar. If you need the extra space inside, the Land Cruiser is the smart pick. But if you can live with slightly tidier dimensions and need off-road capability, go with the 4Runner.

The 4Runner TRD Off-Road i-Force Max is as close as you can get to a Land Cruiser, but if you want even more dramatic savings, a 2026 4Runner SR5 with the $2,000 part-time four-wheel-drive option will serve you just fine. You lose the i-Force Max engine, two-speed transfer case, and some other goodies. But you will only spend $45,865 and still get a viable Land Cruiser alternative.

raw_title: Fabric Molds Could Bring Material-Saving Concrete Beams Within Reach
title: Fabric Molds Could Bring Material-Saving Concrete Beams Within Reach
raw_summary: MIT engineers cast a concrete beam using a sewn fabric mold with one-third the amount of concrete and half as much steel as a conventional beam. Topology optimization is a computer design method that can help engineers design beams using reduced amounts of concrete and steel. But those intricate shapes produced from the tool are often too complex or expensive to pour into conventional rigid molds. The few that have been built have mostly relied on specialized equipment, such as concrete 3D printers or machine-carved molds, equipment that is out of reach in regions where new construction is expected to grow.
summary: MIT engineers cast a concrete beam using a sewn fabric mold with one-third the amount of concrete and half as much steel as a conventional beam. Topology optimization is a computer design method that can help engineers design beams using reduced amounts of concrete and steel.
article_paragraphs: MIT engineers cast a concrete beam using a sewn fabric mold with one-third the amount of concrete and half as much steel as a conventional beam.

Topology optimization is a computer design method that can help engineers design beams using reduced amounts of concrete and steel. But those intricate shapes produced from the tool are often too complex or expensive to pour into conventional rigid molds. The few that have been built have mostly relied on specialized equipment, such as concrete 3D printers or machine-carved molds, equipment that is out of reach in regions where new construction is expected to grow.

Now, MIT engineers have shown that highly efficient beams can be cast in something more accessible: sewn fabric. In a paper published in the Journal of Building Engineering , the team designed and built a 3-meter (about 10-foot) test beam using fabric molds created through an automated pattern-making process. Compared with a conventional beam designed to carry the same weight, the optimized beam used about one-third as much concrete and half as much steel reinforcement. When tested, its measured response was within about 2 percent of what the team’s computer model predicted.

Fabric formwork, in which concrete is poured into a mold made of textile, has been explored for years to create beams that vary in depth, rather than in rectangular shapes common in construction. But because fabric deforms under the weight of wet concrete, that flexibility has made the final shape hard to predict.

“The key realization was that this flexibility is not just a limitation to manage; with the right computational pattern design, it can become a way to produce optimized structural forms,” says Josephine Carstensen, the Gilbert W. Winslow (1937) Career Development Professor in Civil Engineering and senior author of the study.

Fabric molds can also be inexpensive, lightweight, and fast compared to wood or steel molds. “You could sew a formwork together off site, pack it into a box, and bring it to a job site very easily,” says Jackson Jewett PhD ’25, co-author of the study. “We joke that we are developing the H&M of the construction industry.”

“This work addresses concrete’s climate footprint primarily by reducing material demand,” Carstensen says. “Cement production is highly carbon-intensive, so using less concrete is an important part of decarbonizing construction.”

Where new construction happens matters, too. The world’s number of buildings is expected to nearly double by 2050, with about 85 percent of that growth in developing countries, where access to advanced construction equipment is often limited. That is why, Carstensen says, the team focused on an accessible, cost-conscious fabrication approach.

title: 7 Of The Rarest Fox Body Mustangs Ever Built And What They're Worth Today
raw_summary: The Ford Mustang has enjoyed a long career as America's pony car since it debuted in 1964. It lived through the Malaise era, took on competition from all manner of American rivals, and even went on to find considerable success in other markets – no easy feat for a muscle car. Through those years, we've been blessed with a total of seven Mustang generations, but we shouldn't pretend each one was as brilliant as the next. While the first-gen model has gone down as an important slice of American motoring history, the Mustang II that followed is largely best left forgotten. However, the third generation, known as the Fox Body Mustang, rescued the Mustang's reputation as a muscle car and stood the test of time. These cars debuted as '79 model years, and were not replaced until the SN95 cars marched onto the scene for 1994. Throughout those years, an estimated 2.6 million Fox Body Mustangs found owners, making it by far one of the most successful Mustang generations. Among them, though, were some exceedingly rare variants, such as the immensely sought-after 1-of-107 SVT Cobra R, and the 3,003 Feature Cars of '93, and the 1985 Twister II Mustang.

These Mustangs, along with quite a few others that are rarer than many multi-million-dollar super- and hypercars, stand as the rarest Fox Body cars ever produced. Starting with the more common and leaving the rarest for last, here are seven Fox Body Mustang variants with seriously scant production numbers, and how much they're worth today.

If we were to split the Turbo GT up by model year, the '83 Mustang Turbo GT would sit much farther up this list, since only 556 examples made it out of the factory gates. However, with 3,972 examples produced the following year — split between 3,241 hatchbacks and 731 convertibles – the total Turbo GT production comes out to 4,528 examples.

As the name suggests, instead of relying on old-school six- or eight-cylinder lumps that traditionally featured in Mustangs, the Turbo GT took advantage of boost. Under its hood sat a fuel-injected and turbocharged 2.3-liter inline-4, and when fed the correct premium gas, it was good for 145 horsepower and 180 pound-feet of torque. It was actually quite a technically impressive mill for the time, sporting forged aluminum pistons, a lightweight flywheel, valves with a higher heat resistance, and extra oil cooling hardware — this was certainly no half-measure attempt from the Blue Oval engineers.

Ford sadly canned the Turbo GT after the '84 model year. While a smaller four-cylinder engine was no doubt more economical than a naturally aspirated V8, and yet still punchy enough to induce a smile on the face of most drivers, less than 5,000 sales across both model years clearly meant it wasn't a great car to market to the mass market. Such scarcity has not translated into high desirability in the modern day, either, since any recent sales we found on Bring a Trailer barely scraped past $12,000.

The 1992 Ford Mustang Summer Edition, or, to call it by its full name, the 1992 Vibrant Red Mustang LX 5.0 Limited Edition Convertible, was exactly that — a vibrant red drop-top 'Stang. It was powered by a 225-hp, 300-lb-ft, 302-cubic-inch High Output (H.O.) V8, and it debuted halfway through the 1992 model year during the — you guessed it — summer.

Other unique features include a white leather interior with contrasting black stitch-work and a complementary white fabric roof. It was by no means subtle, especially with 16-inch Opal Pearlescent white wheels completing the bold look. Also helping the Summer Edition Mustang differentiate itself from similarly specified but otherwise completely regular Mustangs was a unique decklid spoiler, body-colored mirrors, plus a variety of other Vibrant Red exterior trims too.

title: Is It True That Turbo Engines Need Oil Changes More Often?

article_paragraphs: Forget what your oil life monitor is telling you. Here's when you should change the oil on your turbocharged engine

Like it or not, turbocharged engines are becoming more common. In fact, of the 16.3 million new passenger vehicles sold in the U.S. in 2025, 45% of them were equipped with a turbocharged engine. Automakers are squeezing every drop out power out of smaller engines while trying to reduce fuel consumption, and adding a turbocharger is how many choose to do it. There are trade-offs for these performance perks, though. The most notorious is that there will be some turbo lag, unless you run a supercharger and a turbocharger at once . One trade-off that is mentioned less frequently, though, is that compared to naturally aspirated engines, turbocharged engines require specially formulated oil that needs to be changed more often.

While many enthusiasts might argue that small, four-cylinder engines are not powerful enough, or can't compete with larger V8s, who says we can't have it all? The Jeep Grand Cherokee, Lexus TX350, and the Ford Explorer are great examples of large four-cylinder turbocharged SUVs on the market. Even automakers like Porsche have been using turbocharged engines for years, and even the new Lamborghini Temerario uses a twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V8 .

Despite only becoming mainstream in cars recently, turbocharged engines have been around for years. The concept was patented by Swiss engineer Alfred Buchi in 1905. It took another 20 years for Buchi to get working turbocharged engines into ships and aircrafts.

The transplant of this system from planes, trains and into automobiles first came in 1954, when Volvo and MAN implemented it into trucks, closely followed by the Oldsmobile Cutlass Jetfire 215 CID V8 in 1962. But it was the oil crisis in the mid-'70s that forced automakers to re-think how to make cars more powerful without guzzling more gas. Now, turbocharged engines are a mainstream option. So, how do they work?

Put simply, a turbocharger draws extra air into an engine's cylinders to improve combustion. Exhaust gas from the engine spins a small fan (turbine wheel), which is attached to another spinning part (compression wheel), that feeds the air through. Turbos often have an intercooling system to make the incoming air colder and denser for optimum performance. Oil is a major player in this whole process.

Turbocharged engines rely on engine oil to lubricate moving parts and regulate temperature. Exhaust gases expelled from the engine can be upward of 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit, with fans spinning up to 350,000 RPM. That is a recipe for disaster if the engine is not properly maintained.

While the oil carries heat away from the turbo, frequent exposure to extreme heat is detrimental to oil. When oil is hot, it's thinner and less effective as a lubricant. Increased heat also causes the oil to burn and break down, leading to coking deposits – the build-up of sticky residue inside the narrow passages in the turbocharger.

title: Why Some Cars Will Have More Physical Buttons In The Near Future
raw_summary: Physical buttons could officially make a comeback, and the reasons are straightforward: Drivers pushed back, safety testers sided with them, and even China has proposed making physical controls mandatory for critical functions. After a decade of hybridization, electrification, and shifting buyer tastes, it turns out that more tech doesn't automatically mean a better car. Last year, we looked at how some car brands are rethinking touchscreens and bringing back physical buttons , and that's no longer a vague promise. It's happening in real cars right now. article_paragraphs: Physical buttons could officially make a comeback, and the reasons are straightforward: Drivers pushed back, safety testers sided with them, and even China has proposed making physical controls mandatory for critical functions. After a decade of hybridization, electrification, and shifting buyer tastes, it turns out that more tech doesn't automatically mean a better car.

Last year, we looked at how some car brands are rethinking touchscreens and bringing back physical buttons , and that's no longer a vague promise. It's happening in real cars right now. Ferrari is a good example. Customers criticized the touch controls on the SF90's steering wheel, so Ferrari reworked the design, and the 2027 Amalfi has real buttons. Ferrari is also offering a retrofit to owners stuck with the touch controls, and the Purosangue, the 12Cilindri, and the Roma are among the cars covered.

It isn't just about luxury cars, either. Volkswagen's ID.Tiguan, the ID.4's replacement, arrives in Europe in early 2027 with physical buttons in the cabin, and the Golf GTI and Cupra Born now use physical switches on their steering wheels. Mercedes is doing it, too, on the electric GLC's new steering wheel, and so is Audi with its upcoming A4 E-tron and Q7 E-tron.

So the industry is clearly leaning back toward the tactile. However, its previous move away from buttons isn't easy to undo, so the answer takes more than flipping a switch. It takes a closer look at what drivers actually want and what carmakers can realistically build.

Only partly. The Drive reported that 48% of shoppers in an AutoPacific survey picked dials or buttons over a screen. That's nearly half, yet 60% of respondents also said they like how screens look. Drivers aren't asking for a 1990s dashboard. They want a better balance. As Kelley Blue Book reported, Telemetry's Sam Abuelsamid says physical controls take "a lot of engineering effort," which is why the brands above are keeping screens but bringing buttons back where it counts.

Modern cars pack in a ton of features, and if every one of them got its own button, a luxury interior could start to look like a 747 cockpit. Regulations play a part, too. Since May 2018, new U.S. vehicles under 10,000 pounds have been required to have a backup camera, which puts a screen in the dashboard of nearly every new car. Once there, it makes a convenient home for everything else.

It's not just automakers that are scrutinizing the all-touchscreen dashboard. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has proposed rules that would require physical controls for critical functions in new models starting in 2027. Europe's independent safety testers are pushing in a similar direction. Euro NCAP's 2026 test results came with a headline that says it all: "Buttons are back for basic functions."

Even Jony Ive, designer of the iPhone and the Ferrari Luce, says touchscreens are not the way to go for the future. So it's reasonable to expect a middle ground: screens for the extras, and real buttons for anything you shouldn't have to take your eyes off the road to use.

After falling far short of projected sales, Tesla recently announced it will cease Cybertruck production next year and use the additional factory capacity to build more Cybercabs.

title: Do You Really Need To Change Your Oil Every 5,000 Miles?
raw_summary: Want a sure-fire way to start an argument at a car meet that's even better than trash-talking a Ford Mustang to the owner's face while wearing a bowtie T-shirt? Bring up the topic of oil change intervals. There'll be one guy who claims he hasn't dropped his lube for 20,000 miles because that's what the automaker recommends, and says his motor hasn't exploded yet. Another will swear that you'll send pistons flying if you haven't changed the oil every 5,000 miles. But 5,000 miles might only be a few months of driving for some folks. Do you really need to swap it out that often?
summary: Want a sure-fire way to start an argument at a car meet that's even better than trash-talking a Ford Mustang to the owner's face while wearing a bowtie T-shirt? Bring up the topic of oil change intervals. There'll be one guy who claims he hasn't dropped his lube for 20,000 miles because that's what the automaker recommends, and says his motor hasn't exploded yet.
article_paragraphs: Want a sure-fire way to start an argument at a car meet that's even better than trash-talking a Ford Mustang to the owner's face while wearing a bowtie T-shirt? Bring up the topic of oil change intervals.

There'll be one guy who claims he hasn't dropped his lube for 20,000 miles because that's what the automaker recommends, and says his motor hasn't exploded yet. Another will swear that you'll send pistons flying if you haven't changed the oil every 5,000 miles. But 5,000 miles might only be a few months of driving for some folks. Do you really need to swap it out that often?

The reality is one of those annoying "it depends" answers, so it's no wonder there's confusion around the issue. Years back, changing oil every three months or 3,000 miles was totally normal, just a regular part of a car upkeep schedule. But oil and engine technology were less sophisticated in the middle of the last century. The additives in multigrade oils degrade over time, meaning they provide less protection to engines as the oil gets older, and it needs to be changed more often. If you're driving an older car today on conventional multigrade oil, you're probably still going to want to change it every 5,000 miles, not every 10,000 miles.

But modern, thin, expensive synthetic oils used on newer cars since the 1980s and 1990s last far longer without breaking down. That's the stuff automakers fill their cars' sumps with when they say you can drive 20,000 miles before laying a ratchet on the drain plug. Semi-synthetic oils are hardier than old multigrade oils and cost less than fully synthetic fluid, but still break down faster and need to be changed every 6,000 miles, AAA says .

Just because you've splashed out the cash to splash synthetic oil around your bearings doesn't mean you can safely do 20,000 miles between oil changes. Imagine two identical cars, one sent out for a lifetime of long, gentle, cross-country freeway drives, and the other tasked with spending its days running three-mile errands and barely getting warm. They might have the same engines and the same recommended service intervals, but one car's oil works much harder.

According to Pennzoil lubricant specialist Sean Nguyen on the Bob is the Oil Guy website, those short, urban journeys can be particularly rough on modern direct-injection engines because fuel and moisture can accumulate in the oil. An engine that's allowed to warm up properly can evaporate those contaminants, Nguyen says, but repeated short journeys can prevent that from happening. The result is acid formation, corrosion, and component wear.

But what if you only live a few miles from work? Nguyen recommends taking your car for a 30-minute run every week to help evaporate accumulated fuel and moisture. He also advises sticking with the automaker's official interval, as listed in the handbook. Such driving may fall under the manufacturer's definition of "severe service," which leads to a more frequent oil change interval recommendation.

In the case of a Stellantis SRT vehicle like a Dodge Challenger Hellcat , that means dropping the oil every six months or 6,000 miles. Don't go thinking you only need a lube job once a year if you're only doing 3,000 miles, either. Oil also degrades in cars parked for extended periods.
