title: AI Businesses Still Bleeding Billions
raw_summary: AI is fun and cool when it creates useful things for you or answers tough questions quickly and well (let’s not focus on AI slop and false claims at the moment), but that doesn’t mean AI businesses are financially sustainable or sensible. AI companies are still heavily subsidizing their broad use, with the benefits for them being growing user bases and sky-high valuations. These companies are burning billions of dollars each quarter on the hype and promise that they will rule the world one day (quite literally). OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, reported this week that it had $10.9 billion in operating losses last quarter. That’s up from $10.1 billion in operating losses in the second quarter.

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, reported this week that it had $10.9 billion in operating losses last quarter. That’s up from $10.1 billion in operating losses in the second quarter.

One might think that means not a lot changed, and certainly nothing positive. However, the company’s revenue was actually up by 50% ! So, even with a huge boost in revenue, gigantic losses grew! Furthermore, the company was apparently even using a tool of “last resort” here.

OpenAI started running ads in ChatGPT, something that the company was adamantly trying to avoid. CEO Sam Altman previously called the proposal to run ads “unsettling” and claimed that the company would only go that route as a matter of “last resort.” Well, it seems the company has reached that point of last resort. And that can’t be a good thing, right? Considering that OpenAI is still losing billions of dollars a quarter, it’s even more concerning. What comes after a “last resort” effort to turn finances around?

Frankly, I wish we could spend billions of dollars a quarter to make CleanTechnica into a behemoth of a media organization! That would be amazing — imagine all of the stuff we could do! But what are the chances we’d be losing billions of dollars a quarter in doing so? And how long could we operate like that before external sources of funding stopped covering the bill?
As we know, OpenAI is one of the “leaders” of the AI industry. If it is struggling like this, who isn’t, and what does that mean for the industry overall and where it’s headed?
The one big player that has been raking in the dough in the midst of this enormous AI craze is NVIDIA, and look at what’s now happening there! Where are things going to go with that company?

“The news comes not long after controversy over how OpenAI was projecting its earnings . In October, the company reported an annualized revenue, an estimate of how much money it will earn over a year, of about $50 billion — which was $20 billion short of what it told investors only a month before,” Futurism adds. “The discrepancy was taken as an admission that the business models of AI companies weren’t as robust as their leadership was making them out to be, fueling speculation of an impending bubble .”

raw_title: How Much Power Would An EV's Solar Roof Provide?
title: How Much Power Would An EV's Solar Roof Provide?
raw_summary: When looking at modern EVs, it's all about efficiency. Manufacturers boast about impressive drag coefficient numbers , door handles that retract, large dish-style wheels, teardrop-shaped exterior design, as well as flat, covered underbodies. Furthermore, closed grilles, tapered rooflines, and active aerodynamic features that change the car's aero profile depending on usage are becoming increasingly common. You could also point to cameras in place of side mirrors, low-rolling-resistance tires, and heat pumps that keep the cabin warm in winter without massively draining the battery. The list goes on. However, you might be wondering about solar roofs. By pure logic, an EV covered in solar panels would be more efficient overall, since every mile the sun puts back into the battery is a mile you don't have to plug in for. Or would it? Actual output naturally depends on sunlight, weather conditions, and location. We'll expand on why solar roofs aren't mainstream on EVs later, but for now, let's evaluate how much power an EV's solar roof could theoretically provide.

However, you might be wondering about solar roofs. By pure logic, an EV covered in solar panels would be more efficient overall, since every mile the sun puts back into the battery is a mile you don't have to plug in for. Or would it? Actual output naturally depends on sunlight, weather conditions, and location. We'll expand on why solar roofs aren't mainstream on EVs later, but for now, let's evaluate how much power an EV's solar roof could theoretically provide.

The Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems reports that its prototype solar roof's integrated photovoltaic cells produce approximately 19.5 watts per square foot under nominal conditions. On a 21.5-square-foot roof, by our math, that's roughly 420 watts of peak power. Fraunhofer says its roof could add approximately 6.2 miles of driving range per day in peak summer sun. Over a full year, Fraunhofer's figures for Freiburg, Germany, which assume no shade, point to about 10% more range. Let's take a closer look at how much a solar roof can realistically do within the context of Los Angeles and a Tesla.

Picture a good old Tesla Model 3, one of the most popular EVs offering a leading range . Tesla doesn't list its roof area, so we'll stick with the 21.5-square-foot roof from earlier. Covered in cells rated at 19.5 watts per square foot, that roof would peak at 420 watts. Sunlight is measured in peak sun hours, the number of hours a day that add up to full-strength sun. Let's park it in sun-kissed Los Angeles, where data shows 5.62 peak sun hours a day as an average.

That gets our roof about 2.36 kWh (420 watts x 5.62 hours). In Edmunds' testing, the 2026 Model 3 Standard averaged 0.23 kWh per mile. Divide 2.36 by 0.23, and the roof adds about 10.3 miles a day (without energy losses), around 3% of the car's 321-mile EPA range. Summer's 6.14 hours bump that to about 11.2 miles, while winter's 5.03 drops it to 9.2. Again, those figures ignore the energy lost in charging, the added weight, aero penalties, etc.

Best case, that beats Fraunhofer's 6.2 miles, partly because the Model 3 uses 23 kWh per 100 miles versus Fraunhofer's assumed 27.4. And, for fun, how many Harbor Freight panels for 30 miles a day? That takes 6.9 kWh, or seven Predator 200-watt foldables in LA ($1,609.93 at the time of writing). That's 1,400 watts, more than triple the roof. Using 10-watt Thunderbolt trickle chargers, it's 123, for $5,533.77, plus a power station or inverter to feed the car. Ultimately, even in the best possible scenario, you still need to keep your charging cable handy.

EVs haven't jumped on the solar roof bandwagon for a few reasons. To start, there really isn't much roof to work with (as our Harbor Freight examples showed). A car roof is a small surface, and a panel only hits its rated output in full, direct sunlight. Overcast skies, winter's shorter days, and a layer of road dust all chip away at what the panels make, and a car that regularly parks in a garage collects next to nothing. The aforementioned Fraunhofer estimate is very optimistic, since it assumes a sunny, unshaded day. Solar Team Eindhoven's Stella Terra, a lightweight, student-built off-roader with a smaller battery, drove across Morocco to the Sahara , covering 621 miles without plugging into a charger. Now picture it in Seattle in January.

Then you have the added weight and complexity that comes with these panels. This can work against the efficiency promise, since added weight means the car burns more energy to get moving. Additionally, unless the panels are built flush into the roof, they become one more thing for air to trip over, undermining aero efficiency. These obstacles don't mean solar can't provide supplemental range, but the application isn't as practical as some might perceive it to be.

article_paragraphs: Regular oil changes are still important, even if you're not racking up the miles

Oil is the lifeblood of any internal combustion engine. It needs to be changed on a regular schedule , but oftentimes, drivers only consider the miles between oil changes. Does this mean if you only drive your car 1,000 miles per year and oil changes are recommended every 5,000 miles, you can use the same oil for five years? Not exactly. Oil has a limited lifespan and should generally be changed every six to 12 months, even if you're not driving your car.

You see, even if your car spends most of its time parked in a garage, the engine oil can degrade. Over time, it may begin to oxidize, and small amounts of moisture and dust could enter the oil system, slowly degrading it. So even that 1988 HSV Commodore SS Walkinshaw stored in a garage since new still needs its oil changed before driving it, even though the oil only has 12 miles on it.

How you drive your vehicle may also impact how the oil behaves over time. Even where and how you store your car can have an effect on the oil's life. For example, cars stored outside have to deal with fluctuating temperatures, which can accelerate the degradation compared to a car that's stored inside. If those rare drives you do take are short, it's possible the oil hasn't heated up enough to eliminate any moisture that may have found its way in.

It's not just reduced lubrication properties that can impact an oil's effectiveness if it's left to sit for too long. As moisture builds up in the oil when a car is parked for an extended period, it can trigger some corrosion in vital engine components. A little corrosion from driving on salty roads on the underside of your car probably isn't a big deal. However, corrosion inside the engine can be, and unless you're an expert engine builder, you probably won't be able to open up your engine to clean it. Fuel efficiency is also likely to be adversely affected by aging oil.

To prevent your old oil from looking like it hasn't been changed for 37,000 miles , consider the time between oil changes, not just the mileage. Changing engine oil every six to 12 months is a good idea, including the weekender you drive just a couple of times per month. Synthetic oil is more resilient than conventional oil and will last longer, but even so, regular changes are recommended.

There are a few easy ways to tell whether your vehicle is in dire need of an oil change. Check the color of the oil on the dipstick. If it has turned dark and no longer looks like the liquid honey it did when it was new, changing the oil is a smart move. Any signs of contamination, debris, or sludge are also a good indication that it's time to head to your local parts store to buy some fresh oil.

raw_title: Why Some Traffic Lights Have A Yellow Border
title: Why Some Traffic Lights Have A Yellow Border
raw_summary: If you're anything like me, in addition to scanning the road for distracted drivers and pedestrians, you also scan signs and roadsides for anything that could potentially be a red-light or speed camera . It feels like Big Brother is always watching and waiting for you to pass the 11 mph over-the-speed-limit threshold or to miss the "no right on red" sign nowadays, so there are a lot of things fighting for your attention when you're behind the wheel. If you've noticed that some traffic signals have a reflective yellow border while scanning your surroundings, you may wonder what they're for, but the simple fact that you've noticed them means they've served their purpose. Those reflective yellow borders that surround some traffic signals have several intended purposes, including boosting signal visibility at night time, getting the attention of drivers with color vision deficiencies, and ensuring motorists are aware of an upcoming intersection , even when the lights are inoperative — in a power outage, for instance. The border is a simple and low-cost feature that has been proven to increase road safety.

Those reflective yellow borders that surround some traffic signals have several intended purposes, including boosting signal visibility at night time, getting the attention of drivers with color vision deficiencies, and ensuring motorists are aware of an upcoming intersection , even when the lights are inoperative — in a power outage, for instance. The border is a simple and low-cost feature that has been proven to increase road safety.

A 2005 study titled " Safety Impact of Increased Traffic Signal Backboards Conspicuity " found that adding a three-inch yellow micro-prismatic retroreflective sheeting around the outer edge of a traffic signal backboard could reduce collisions by about 15%. The reflective material not only makes spotting traffic signals easier at night, but also in the daytime, particularly when signals are backlit at sunrise and sunset, as well as signals that are surrounded by reflective buildings and other visual distractions. The implementation of reflective yellow borders is not federally required at every intersection, so state and local transportation agencies usually decide where to install them.

The U.S. Department of Transportation's Federal Highway Administration considers adding a one-to-three-inch yellow retroreflective border to traffic signal backplates a "human factors enhancement of traffic signal visibility, conspicuity, and orientation." It cites the modification as a very low-cost, proven safety treatment, with the only potential concern being the integrity of the signal support structure in severe winds, which should be considered if adding a backplate to a signal in a wind-prone area.

article_paragraphs: The findings indicate where adaptive measures are needed most around the United States.

Global warming, the observed increase in the Earth’s average global surface temperature since preindustrial (1850-1900) times, currently stands at around 1.63 degrees Celsius . While this number is expected to continue to rise, local temperatures will not go up uniformly around the world. In regions where warming trends are most pronounced, local adaptation and resilience measures will be especially critical to minimizing risks to ecosystems, agricultural productivity, the built environment, human health, and economic well-being.

To that end, a new open-access study in the journal Scientific Data identifies the highest-risk regions for warming within the United States. Using data from well-known, high-resolution climate and weather datasets ( MERRA2 and ERA5 ) covering the years 1980-2022, researchers at the MIT Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy ( CS3 ) report global warming-attributed trends in monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature for every U.S. state.

The study finds that Alaska, Utah, New Mexico, Colorado, and Nevada have experienced the strongest average warming trends; the lowest occurred in Hawaii, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Arkansas. Across the country, warming trends were most pronounced during the summer and fall, particularly in September and November. Alaska has the highest historical maximum daily temperature warming (an average of 2.5 C of monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature increase per degree of global warming), while Hawaii has the lowest average historical warming, at 0.8 C.

The authors expect that barring unforeseen local anomalies, these state-by-state temperature trends will continue unabated as ongoing global emissions from human activities continue to raise the average global temperature.

“Based on these results, we encourage decision-makers to assess states that have undergone the steepest increases in maximum and minimum daily temperatures, and identify where continued trends would indicate a rapid progression toward thresholds beyond which natural and managed resources, ecosystems, and infrastructure can function safely,” says MIT CS3 Deputy Director C. Adam Schlosser , a co-author of the study. “In such cases, triaging and adaptive measures would take a high priority. By directing resources to where they are needed most, state and regional planners could significantly reduce climate-related physical and financial risks.”

Unlike previous efforts to report temperature trends across the United States, this study aggregates average maximum, minimum, and mean daily temperature data at the state level for each month of the year, providing actionable information for planners in government, industry, and civil society.

raw_title: The 5 Worst Rebadges In Automotive History
title: The 5 Worst Rebadges In Automotive History
raw_summary: Platform sharing is one of the most common strategies in the automotive industry, and the best way to reduce R&D costs by taking advantage of the economy of scale. While shared underpinnings can lead to successful models with distinct identities, there is also the case of rebadging where brands sacrifice their styling integrity in order to enter new segments or comply with regulations in different markets around the world. Rebadged models are often criticized by automotive enthusiasts, so we decided to gather the five worst examples of badge engineering we could think of in a single story. With countless cases to choose from, compiling the list proved to be tough. Still, we tried our best to choose vehicles that did very little to adapt into the lineup of the brand they migrated to, and didn't make sense from a branding standpoint. Think Cadillac Cimarron and Honda Crossroad. Out of the five spots in the wall of shame, one model comes from the 1980s, two from the 1990s, and two from the early 2010s. So let's check them out in chronological order.

Rebadged models are often criticized by automotive enthusiasts, so we decided to gather the five worst examples of badge engineering we could think of in a single story.

With countless cases to choose from, compiling the list proved to be tough. Still, we tried our best to choose vehicles that did very little to adapt into the lineup of the brand they migrated to, and didn't make sense from a branding standpoint. Think Cadillac Cimarron and Honda Crossroad. Out of the five spots in the wall of shame, one model comes from the 1980s, two from the 1990s, and two from the early 2010s. So let's check them out in chronological order.

Cadillac is positioned as a premium brand, going against the likes of BMW and Mercedes-Benz. Still, there was a time that General Motors executives decided it would make sense to rebadge Chevrolet's entry-level sedan as a potential rival to the BMW 3-Series E30 and the Mercedes 190E W201. The Cadillac Cimarron didn't only share the J-body platform and powertrains with the Chevrolet Cavalier, but also carried over most of its design.

Changes were limited to the Cadillac-specific grille, extra chrome trim, wraparound taillights, alloy wheels, and the optional vinyl roof. Inside, the Caddy came fitted with more heavily bolstered seats upholstered in leather, fake aluminum or fake wood trim, and more generous standard equipment that included air conditioning. Still, the biggest problem was pricing. Back in 1982, the Cadillac started at around $12k when its humble Chevrolet twin could be yours for $7k. This limited its target group to buyers who didn't care about the essence of the vehicle and only wanted the bragging rights of owning a Cadillac.

The Japanese market has many automotive oddities, but only a few can give you a brain freeze like the first generation of the Honda Crossroad. The off-roader was introduced in 1993 and remains the only V8-powered Honda ever made. However, as you might have guessed from the photo, it is not actually a Honda. The Crossroad is nothing more than a Land Rover Discovery Series I with Honda emblems on the grille, tailgate, steering wheel, and center caps.

The rest of the bodywork, interior, V8 engine, full-time 4WD system, and ladder-frame chassis are carried over from the British 4x4. It was available in three-door guise with five seats, or as a five-door model with seven seats. Predictably, the Honda Crossroad struggled to find traction with Japanese buyers, who were shocked to see a Discovery sitting in Honda showrooms alongside true Hondas such as the Civic, the Accord, and the original NSX .

Back in the '90s, Kia wanted to change course and produce a sportscar to compete with the Mazda MX-5. While the young brand didn't have the funds to develop a model on its own at the time, an amazing opportunity arose when Lotus decided to discontinue one of its nameplates. The front-wheel-drive Lotus Elan M100 went out of production in 1995, after suffering a defeat from the aforementioned rear-wheel-drive MX-5 NA. Interestingly, Kia decided to acquire the tooling to produce the Elan, along with the license to sell it with its own badges.

This signaled the birth of the Kia Elan in Korea, which was also exported to Japan as the Kia Vigato . Besides the emblems, changes in the Kia version were limited to unique taillight clusters, new wheels, and a revised suspension setup with increased ground clearance. The fiberglass body and steel backbone chassis were carried over, but the Isuzu-sourced engine of the original was swapped for a Kia-built naturally aspirated 1.8-liter mill. Priced at ₩27,500,000, the Lotus-derived sportscar was one of the most expensive models in the Korean market and failed to attract a large number of buyers.

article_paragraphs: The year of the robotaxi rolls on. Just after writing about Zoox expanding its robotaxi service in Las Vegas , I see news that Zoox is entering Atlanta!
“Our initial rollout will focus on the Northwest region of Atlanta, near Atlantic Station, Woodward, and Home Park. We will expand throughout the year as our testing progresses,” Zoox shares .

To start with, in order to work out any bugs and avoid controversy, the service can only be used by Zoox employees, family members, and friends. But that should change fairly soon. “We look forward to opening our waitlist for Atlanta in the coming months, ahead of the launch of our Zoox Explorers early rider program.”

I do find it interesting that Zoox, Waymo, and Tesla are all in a sort of fast (but sort of small) expansion phase at the same time. They each keep adding more cities, but with quite limited geographic ranges and vehicle fleets. Is it all the early budding of robotaxi services that will bloom into giant networks? Or is it companies rushing to try to prove their viability and build up economies of scale, but which might not actually be financially viable and profitable in the long run — or even next year? We’ll have to wait to see. In the meantime, it’s certainly exciting each time a new area is opened up and more electric robotaxis hit the road.

In case you have forgotten where Zoox is in operation, the company informs us: “Atlanta marks our newest testing market for the robotaxi. This is in addition to testing in Austin and Miami , our public service in Las Vegas , and our Zoox Explorers early rider program in San Francisco .”

Also of note is the fact that Zoox didn’t just decide last month to go to Atlanta and rush into the market. It has been laying the groundwork for this launch for about a year and a half in the city. “We started operations in Atlanta in the Spring of 2025, using our testing fleet to map and learn about local driving behaviors, weather patterns, and the city infrastructure. Since then, we have been steadily expanding our driving capabilities, including beginning autonomous driving, and growing our geofence, fleet size, and team to prepare for this next stage of testing.” Zoox explains further how this is central to how Zoox operates:

“Zoox has always been thoughtful and measured in our approach to rolling out autonomous technology at every level. Before we even hit the road and begin driving with our testing fleet in any capacity, we first engage with local and state officials and regulators. Our philosophy is ‘no surprises’ as we lay the foundations for future service markets.

“Along with engaging with local and state officials and regulators, we also love partnering with the community. Workforce development starts long before a first job. That’s why we’re partnering with @Promise Center to help local youth learn, grow, and prepare for their futures in a safe, supportive environment. This partnership reflects our commitment to the Atlanta community. We’re excited to continue investing in the next generation and the future of this city.”

article_paragraphs: We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking , and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

Originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive ( and supremely affordable ) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis .

To be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow users to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

There are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino , or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

But above the exotic and the absurd, Matt McEntegart’s custom 1979 Chevrolet El Camino, named the “SS Monte Mino,” brings the trophy home. McEntegart, a Florida native, spent thousands of hours designing and fabricating the build. While the SS Monte Mino wears an El Camino shell, it’s anything but stock, taking parts and inspiration from Corvettes and Monte Carlos.

The SS Monte Mino rides on a modified sixth-generation Corvette chassis. McEntegart stretched the El Camino’s wheelbase by 12 inches and crafted a custom Monte Carlo–inspired wide-body kit using foam prototypes and molds.

The Frankenstein car is powered by a modified Chevy V-8 engine, complete with exposed velocity stacks and performance upgrades. The car practically sits on top of its 22-inch gold wheels thanks to a custom air suspension system.

McEntegart’s low-slung custom ute is a sight to behold, and it truly looks like it was born to speed down a bright orange Hot Wheels track. The exterior is painted in a dark maroon color and uses red-tinted forged carbon-fiber panels to bring out the details along the bodywork.

Inside, the car is all-out retro, with a custom red leather interior to match the exterior red accents. The seats feature a red, black, and gray plaid pattern, and the center console seamlessly blends a few bits of modern tech with the car’s vintage-styled interior.

The SS Monte Mino will be transformed into a 1:64-scale die-cast Hot Wheels car and join the brand’s Garage of Legends, where it’ll sit among past global winners. The scale model will eventually be available to buy worldwide.

Alayna Wilkening grew up reading motorsport magazines and following her grandpa around his Chevrolet dealership's showroom floor. In true Hoosier fashion, her first car was a hot pink custom cardboard "Fiero-vette" for her kindergarten Kindy 500 race. She now autocrosses a 1994 Miata with her dad, which she learned to drive the night before her first event. Alayna went to Indiana University and graduated with a degree in journalism and a minor in graphic design. As a testament to her great taste in cars, her first real one was a metallic orange 2007 Chevy HHR, which she lovingly called "The Dumptruck."

title: Is Using Launch Control Hard On Your Car, Especially If You Use It A Lot?
raw_summary: The sheer breadth of ability in modern performance cars is staggering. Take the seventh generation of the monstrous BMW M5 . Critics love to point out that the plug-in hybrid super sedan is a bit porky, yet it still hits 60 mph in 3 seconds, pulls 0.98 g on the skidpad, and runs the quarter-mile in under 11 seconds in Car and Driver 's testing. When it's done embarrassing sports cars, it'll carry five adults in comfort, and it's wrapped in more tech and safety kit than most of us will ever learn to use. Critics love to point out that the plug-in hybrid super sedan is a bit porky, yet it still hits 60 mph in 3 seconds, pulls 0.98 g on the skidpad, and runs the quarter-mile in under 11 seconds in Car and Driver 's testing.
article_paragraphs: The sheer breadth of ability in modern performance cars is staggering. Take the seventh generation of the monstrous BMW M5 . Critics love to point out that the plug-in hybrid super sedan is a bit porky, yet it still hits 60 mph in 3 seconds, pulls 0.98 g on the skidpad, and runs the quarter-mile in under 11 seconds in Car and Driver 's testing. When it's done embarrassing sports cars, it'll carry five adults in comfort, and it's wrapped in more tech and safety kit than most of us will ever learn to use.

That kind of performance doesn't come down to silly power and no control. A big part of how heavy machines like the M5 get off the line so violently is launch control. In a combustion car, the system caps the revs while you hold the brake, then distributes power so the tires don't go up in smoke once you let go.

The idea behind launch control is to balance the power delivery with traction, so you can go as fast as possible without spinning the wheels. So, is launch control hard on your car? The short answer is that the system itself isn't.

Every full-throttle start puts a heavy load on the drivetrain, axles, and tires all at once. Do that over and over, and the clutch, transmission, and the rest of the drivetrain take the brunt of it. None of those parts are cheap, so if you've made a habit of launching at every green light, it's worth knowing what it's actually doing to your car.

Automakers are aware that repeated launches can be a problem, and that is why they advise you on how to use the feature. The BMW M4 owner's manual (available on ManualsLib ) bluntly warns: "The use of Launch Control causes premature component wear." Kia's Stinger manual adds that leaning on it constantly "can put enormous stress on transmission, engine, and drive shafts." Both BMW and Kia also want owners to hold off until a new car's break-in period is done.

The Stinger disables launch control once its transmission fluid gets too hot, and BMW M won't allow repeated launches under certain conditions — you have to drive a bit for it to function again. Even the wait at the line is capped, with exhaust temperature restricting launch control to five seconds on the manual M3 and M4. Lexus caps how many times the LFA's launch control can be used, and the car's manual (hosted on ManualsLib ) tells owners to "cruise at a normal speed for approximately 10 minutes" before launching again.

For the M3 and M4, though, BMW M says there's "no limitation of the launch control's availability over its lifetime." Porsche Livermore , a Porsche dealership, says launch control is "engineered for thrills, not daily commutes." The quickest factory cars that can hit 60 mph in 3 seconds or less usually rely on launch control to reach those silly numbers. Without it, acceleration can be noticeably slower. The Porsche 911 Carrera GTS T-Hybrid, for example, reached 60 mph in 2.5 seconds with launch control in Car and Driver 's testing, compared with 3.1 seconds when accelerating from a 5-mph crawl.

Let's use a 2009 Nissan GT-R as an example. According to Cars.com , with stability control off and launch control on, one owner ended up with a $20,000 repair bill the warranty didn't cover. Though transmission failures were very rare, Nissan released new launch-control software that went easier on the transaxle.

title: Diesel Prices Used To Be Cheaper Than Gas
raw_summary: Many Americans are not particularly happy about the country's soaring gas prices. Currently, the national average for diesel is $6.06 a gallon, and gasoline is at $3.87, according to AAA . While tensions in the Middle East have some part to play in increasing global crude oil prices, diesel being more expensive than gasoline is not something new in the country. In fact, "On-highway diesel fuel prices have been higher than regular-grade gasoline prices, on a dollar-per-gallon basis, almost continuously since September 2004," according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) . Before that diesel was typically cheaper than gas, except during winter months when demand was high, as the fuel is commonly used in home heating.

article_paragraphs: Many Americans are not particularly happy about the country's soaring gas prices. Currently, the national average for diesel is $6.06 a gallon, and gasoline is at $3.87, according to AAA . While tensions in the Middle East have some part to play in increasing global crude oil prices, diesel being more expensive than gasoline is not something new in the country.

In fact, "On-highway diesel fuel prices have been higher than regular-grade gasoline prices, on a dollar-per-gallon basis, almost continuously since September 2004," according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) . Before that diesel was typically cheaper than gas, except during winter months when demand was high, as the fuel is commonly used in home heating.

Relatively high demand across Europe, China, India, and the United States is one of the reasons why diesel got more expensive than gasoline over the years. Beyond the usual supply-demand dynamics, other variables, like the push for low-sulfur diesels, also raised the fuel's production and distribution costs, due to the additional refining involved. Another contributing factor, per the EIA, is the federal excise tax for on-highway diesel, which is 6 cents a gallon higher than gasoline. Throw geopolitics and supply constraints into the mix, and you start to see why prices are so high.

The rate at which diesel prices rose when compared to AAA's data from the same time last year is quite staggering. While gasoline's national average was $3.08 a gallon, diesel's was at $3.76, meaning diesel jumped more than 60% during that period. And that's despite the U.S. running a diesel surplus and refineries churning out at near-maximum capacity with 97% utilization. So, why are diesel prices so high?

Despite less than 3% of U.S. passenger cars using diesel, the economy, whether it's shipping, logistics, agriculture, or construction, relies heavily on diesel. Compared to gasoline, diesel is a bit more inelastic, meaning price changes won't necessarily impact its demand. "People still drive a lot when gas prices go up, but consumers do vote with their pocketbook, and they will cut back on trips and stuff," says Gregg Ibendahl, an associate professor of agricultural economics at Kansas State University (via Scientific American ). "When it comes to diesel fuel, though, it's not that way at all," Ibendahl continues, "Diesel price is $2.50 higher than what it was in spring, but that's not going to stop a single farmer from running their combine out there."

According to another EIA report, high crude oil prices and reduced refining activity in Russia, China, and the Middle East are part of the reason for the rising diesel prices in recent months. Ukraine targeted many of Russia's refineries, China suspended its fuel exports to protect its domestic stocks, and the Strait of Hormuz ... well, you know what's happening there. This naturally increases demand for exports from the United States, as the country is one of the largest producers of refined oil products in the world. If you weren't aware, the U.S. exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day. Domestic consumption is around 3.6 million barrels per day, and the country refines roughly 5.3 million barrels per day, according to the American Action Forum . So, why not cut the exports like China did? Won't more domestic supply reduce diesel prices?

An export ban won't necessarily make things any better, reckons the aforementioned American Action Forum. According to its report, while an export ban may initially cool wholesale prices in the Gulf Coast (where major U.S. diesel production is concentrated), lower prices may not translate to other parts of the country because of logistics and infrastructure constraints.

In the case of New England, for example, it's much cheaper to import diesel from Canada than to source it domestically. The West Coast, Hawaii, and Alaska also import diesel to supplement their domestic supply. A sustained ban would eventually force U.S. refiners to cut back on production as they might face trouble finding options to absorb the excess supply. If refineries reduce production, it would drive up prices of all petroleum products, including diesel, which defeats the whole point of having the ban in the first place.

title: BMW Pays Tribute To Alex Zanardi With A Very Special M3
raw_summary: The racing icon and Paralympian died in May 2026, and this special BMW M3 commemorates what would have been his 60th birthday Six months after racing driver and Paralympic champion Alex Zanardi passed away, BMW Italy is paying tribute to him with a special one-off M3 Competition. article_paragraphs: The racing icon and Paralympian died in May 2026, and this special BMW M3 commemorates what would have been his 60th birthday

Six months after racing driver and Paralympic champion Alex Zanardi passed away, BMW Italy is paying tribute to him with a special one-off M3 Competition. The Italian driver raced with BMW for several years, and although he's no longer around to see what BMW has built for him, the tribute car has some special touches we're sure he'd be proud to see.

The most personal reference to Zanardi is the pineapple motif on the car's C-pillar. The pineapple became a permanent fixture on Zanardi's helmets and served as his good-luck charm. BMW Italy didn't just slap on the multi-colored pineapple and call it a day. The special one-off M3 Competition is finished in matte white and includes red accents on the front splitter, as well as the colors of the M division running along the sides.

There are also red and blue accents on the hood as well as "BMW M3 G80 2026 / 60th Tribute Alex Zanardi" script on the hood and front doors celebrating what would have been Zanardi's 60th birthday. A blacked-out rear bumper completes the look. Several interior elements distinguish this one-off from a regular, run-of-the-mill G80 M3. The same pineapple motif found on the C-pillar has been embroidered into the headrests. The seats are trimmed in black Alcantara with colorful center inserts, a feature that's been carried through to the door cards. Red stitching has been added to the Alcantara center console to again pay tribute to Zanardi.

Zanardi was a successful go-kart racer and made his open-wheeled racing debut in the 1988 Italian Formula Three Championship. He worked his way up the ranks and, in 1991, made his Formula 1 debut. He also competed in the top tier of motorsport in 1992, 1993, and 1994 before transitioning to the PPG Indy Car World Series in 1996 with Target Ganassi Racing. He enjoyed almost immediate success with the team and finished third in the driver's championship.

The following year, Zanardi raced in the CART series with Ganassi, claiming five race wins and seven podiums, walking away with the championship title. He backed this up the following year by winning the 1998 CART championship in dominant fashion. Zanardi again competed in the CART series in 2001, but he lost both his legs in a devastating crash during the 2001 American Memorial 500. For most, an injury like this would have ended their racing career.

However, Zanardi didn't let the injury hinder him, and he returned to race in 2003 with BMW in the European Touring Car Championship. He continued to race for BMW until his retirement from motorsport in 2019. Zanardi didn't just make a name for himself on the racetrack. He famously took up para-cycling after his 2001 crash and went on to win four gold medals at the 2012 London and 2016 Rio de Janeiro Paralympic Games .

title: Huawei set to challenge Tesla Powerwall with new, 20 kW home battery
raw_summary: This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in , and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark. Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

article_paragraphs: This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in , and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark.

Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes.

“We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” said Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.”

Huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That’s enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you’ll want to keep going if you’re preparing for more than a day or two without power.

If that sounds like you, Luterra’s got you covered. T he modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems , with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel.

Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB ( about the same as my Mac mini ). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away.

Alas, the Luterra S2 probably won’t be making its way to the US anytime soon – but fear not! If you’re shopping for a Tesla Powerwall alternative that won’t help fund the absolute worst people in politics, there are a number of great home battery systems on the market that can deliver backup power, store your solar energy, and keep your home running when the grid goes down. We’ve rounded up some of the best alternatives right here .

raw_title: The US Is Auctioning Seabed Near American Samoa. A $3 Million Bid Will Not Build a Mine.
title: The US Is Auctioning Seabed Near American Samoa. A $3 Million Bid Will Not Build a Mine
raw_summary: On November 19, the US Marine Minerals Administration is scheduled to auction mineral rights covering about 31.5 million acres of seabed near American Samoa. The two areas have minimum bids of $3 million apiece, with 20-year lease terms. It is an impressive area and a modest opening price for a prospective new metals industry. The difference between the two numbers helps explain what the sale is actually offering. The winning bidder will acquire a position from which to study mineral deposits and seek subsequent permissions. The government has said explicitly that an issued lease does not authorize commercial harvesting. It allows preliminary work such as mapping, while physical exploration, testing and mining require additional plans and approvals. The lease does not establish reserves, a collector that can work for years, a processing plant or buyers willing to pay enough for the metals.

The announcement is being treated as an American critical-minerals milestone. Investors should pay close attention to the difference between a government auction and an operating mining project. A mineral lease can have speculative value long before a profitable business exists.
In my new TFIE Strategy Briefing on the American Samoa auction , I examine how federal leasing can advance while the integrated business case remains weak.

The acreage has no direct relationship to the amount of commercially recoverable metal. The final federal notice describes northern and southern areas of roughly 16.3 million and 15.2 million acres. They are regulatory boundaries. A mining company needs deposit-grade and abundance data, continuity, recoverable tonnage, processing recoveries and a market price that leaves a margin after all the offshore and downstream costs.

The geology is becoming better understood. In April 2026, US Geological Survey scientists deployed 38 box cores in the Samoa Basin, of which 36 yielded enough material for nodule-density measurements. The expedition report is useful new evidence about the region. It is an expedition summary rather than a reserve statement for either lease area. Mineral distributions vary within the sampled region, and the better-studied Clarion-Clipperton Zone is not an adequate substitute for American Samoa’s own geological evidence.

Collection creates another set of costs. Impossible Metals proposes autonomous vehicles that select nodules and return to a support vessel. The Metals Company uses a more mature crawler-and-riser approach that has demonstrated recovery at pilot scale. Both must turn offshore demonstrations into dependable annual production, with maintenance, ship time, recovery systems and delays included. Their technologies should not be assigned the same engineering maturity, but neither has proved a profitable integrated mining-and-processing business.

In 2025, metallurgical engineer Lyle Trytten and I completed an independent techno-economic assessment commissioned by the National Ocean Protection Coalition. We examined both collection approaches, offshore operations, processing, metal markets and financial sensitivities. We judged commercial viability within the following 15 years highly unlikely. A new leasing process has not supplied the operating and financial evidence that was missing in that assessment.

The two areas have minimum bids of $3 million apiece, with 20-year lease terms.

If only there was someone with a whiteboard who could break down the physics and legitimacy of the new Roadster and its many engineering feats. That's precisely what Jason Fenske from YouTube's Engineering Explained set out to do. Because specifications of the Roadster aren't available yet, including weight distribution, dimensions, and so on, Fenske had to improvise with assumptions. But the gist is: the new Tesla Roadster reveal appears to be legit, though with a few caveats.

Fenske begins by analyzing the Roadster's fan-assisted aerodynamics. For the Roadster to stay upside down (as seen in the demo), the estimated pressure differential is around 11.5 kilopascals (kPa), — an 11.5% vaccum — achieved with help from fans that suck air out of a small area underneath the car that's sealed using deployable skirts.

That 11.5 kPa is the pressure difference between the top of the car (1 atmosphere, or approximately 100 kPa) and the bottom of the car (88.5 kPa), arrived at using the downforce figures from Tesla's demo and Fenske's assumption of the Roadster's skirt area. While he reckons the system could theoretically generate up to 90,000 kilograms of downforce (if that 88.5 kPa is brought down to zero, i.e., 100% vacuum), the car only needed an 11.5% vacuum to stay upside down.

Next up, Fenske breaks down the Roadster's brief flight and kickflip demonstration. For that, the mass flow rate of the 250 kilograms of available nitrogen (stored at 10,000 pounds per square inch in the two storage tanks) is determined using rocket science and a few assumptions. Dividing the available mass of nitrogen (250 kilos) by the mass flow rate (37 kg/s) reveals that the Roadster (in Rocket spec) can hover in the air for about seven seconds. Fenske reckons that both stunts are possible, considering each took around four seconds to complete. Whether Tesla used larger storage tanks or a lighter shell is debatable, but the demo appears to be plausible.

As for the 0-60 times, Fenske starts with the Base Roadster, which is yet to be confirmed as a production model. In any case, plugging the variables (most of which are assumptions) into a fancy equation reveals that the Base Roadster can achieve a maximum acceleration of 0.99 g. This translates to a 0-60 time of around 2.76 seconds. On the Performance variant, which comes equipped with the fans, Fenske arrives at an estimated 2.3 g and 1.2 seconds for its 0-60. However, he does mention caveats, as variables like the friction coefficient and pressure distribution can influence the final number.

To see whether the Thrust version can actually run a 0-60 of 0.81 seconds, he connects the model's acceleration of 3.37 g to the mass flow rate of nitrogen (37 kg/s). According to Fenske, if you only need around 40 kilos of nitrogen to deliver 1 g for 1.0 seconds, the 200-liter storage tank has enough and more to hit 3.37 g. As for the Rocket variant, Fenske estimates a 0-60 time of 0.5 seconds, pulling a whopping 5.5 g based on his assumptions.

At the end of the day, this event was a great marketing stunt. And that's pretty much how Fenske sees it, because the Roadster's upside-down trick has a few real-world nuances to consider. For instance, the skirts are a wear item, as are the fans. Using the McMurtry as an example, he explains that debris can still enter the fans no matter how efficiently the system filters out the air. Also, the downforce levels depend on the surface, and the demo uses an ideal setup, according to Fenske, which is far from the typical unevenness of actual road surfaces. So real-world performance may be different.

title: What Do All The Flags Mean In Racing?
raw_summary: Some are obvious, while others have different meanings depending on where you see them. Racing can seem pretty simple on its face. Behind that simple premise are several layers of safety methodology to keep everyone, both drivers and spectators, alive and well. Perhaps the simplest form of that safety strategy comes in the form of flags.

article_paragraphs: Some are obvious, while others have different meanings depending on where you see them.

Racing can seem pretty simple on its face. Cars go around a track, and the one in front at the end is the winner. Behind that simple premise are several layers of safety methodology to keep everyone, both drivers and spectators, alive and well. Perhaps the simplest form of that safety strategy comes in the form of flags.

Rather than requiring a driver to read a sign or understand some sort of hand signal or light pattern, a flag is straightforward. It can tell drivers all sorts of things about the race, the track, conditions, or potential hazards just around the corner.

The kicker here is that the flags don't always mean the same thing from one motorsport to another. What might mean "Go" in NASCAR could simply mean the danger is clear in Formula One. Today, we're going to break down the most common flags, what they mean, how they keep drivers safe, and even get into some of the rarer ones you might not ever see.

Most race courses use three main colors to denote the most important signals. Green typically means "go." In NASCAR, it's the flag waved at the beginning of the race. In Formula One, the race starts with green lights rather than a flag, but the green does link the two in the event of a caution or accident. When a race needs to be restarted after such an event, both NASCAR and Formula One use a green flag to get things going again.

Yellow flags are common in both series as well. Generally speaking, the yellow flag means "caution." In NASCAR, the field slows down and gathers behind the pace car. In Formula One, things are a touch different. One waved flag requires drivers to slow down, cease overtaking, and be ready to change direction. A second yellow flag in F1 tells the drivers to significantly slow down and be ready to stop. Both only come out when there's a crash or debris on the track. Sometimes drivers will see a "local yellow," where only one section of the track requires drivers to slow down, while racing continues on the rest of the track.

Perhaps most importantly, there's also a red flag. Much like a red light on a roadway tells drivers to stop, a red flag means the same thing. The flag usually tells all drivers to stop where they are. It can also mean to follow the flaggers' instructions and return to the pits slowly and safely. It's the same story in F1.
Both series and, frankly, most racing series use the same finishing lap signal: a checkered flag. It's the most well-known flag and tells every driver that the race is over.

It's the Yardmax YE0610, a 1,432-pound mini-excavator with a host of available attachments, from a claw to a grading bucket and rake. Better yet, you might just be able to scoot on down to your local Tractor Supply and pick one up.

That said, Yardmax's diminutive earth mover isn't the smallest thing in the mini-excavator market. In fact, if you want to get crazy with your tiny tools, Honda and Komatsu once teamed up to make what may very well be the cutest little digging machine ever.

You've seen the big stuff. You know, the massive, earth-moving heavy construction equipment required to build a modern highway . Monstrous bulldozers, cold milling machines, and long-necked dinosaur-ish excavators are all part of the process. Some of these dirt-munching excavators can get properly huge, with the biggest examples tipping the scales at over 2 million pounds. Yes, you read that right.

Other excavators, however, go for more of a park-it-in-your-garage footprint. That's what the Yardmax YE0610 mini-excavator is all about. At just 27.5 inches wide, the wee digging machine's width takes up considerably less floor space than a common go-kart. Even with the canopy installed on the YE0610-575003 model, the mini-excavator is 62.4 inches tall and 1,674 pounds. Opt for the topless base YE0610, and that weight drops to 1,432 pounds. Not exactly a 2-million-pound earth mover.

Okay, so it's cute. Can it dig? Yardmax asserts the YE0610 can dig up to 47.2 inches deep, or just under four feet. Then there are the attachments. Depending on the model, the Yardmax can use a claw, grading bucket, or rake for your digging, filling, clearing, and leveling tasks. As far as power goes, the mini-excavator features a 306-cc engine capable of hustling the little machine at a cautious 1-mph pace. As expected, the excavator can rotate 360 degrees, regardless of track position.

This wee workhorse might be one of the wildest things Tractor Supply sells. Then again, it might not be. After all, this is a retailer that also offers a teeny tiny minibike to awaken your inner child .

As of this writing, the Yardmax YE0610, complete with its removable canopy, grading bucket, and rake, is for sale at Tractor Supply for $6,999.99. Want to save a couple hundred bucks on your backyard digging machine? The same setup is available at Walmart for $6,799. Of course, if you'd rather go in another direction entirely, Tractor Supply also sells a Power Wheels-esque mini truck . Your mini truck won't likely do any excavating for you, though.

article_paragraphs: From shared hybrid fours to a Yamaha-developed V10, the answer depends on which Lexus you’re looking at.

When buyers compare Lexus with Toyota, a recurring question might surface – are you paying extra for a more premium version of the same car, or are there any differences under the skin? Well, the answer depends on the model.

It is no secret that Toyota leverages shared architectures across its brands to maximize efficiency. As a result, most Lexus sedans, crossovers, and SUVs use the same core powertrains as the equivalent Toyota models.

A prime example of a shared mill is the hybrid naturally aspirated 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine that can be found in the Toyota RAV4 and Lexus NX 350h siblings, as well as the Toyota Camry and Lexus ES 350h sedans. Likewise, the more potent turbocharged 2.4-liter four-cylinder engine powers the Toyota Grand Highlander and Lexus TX 350 among others.

Moving up the ladder, the twin-turbo 3.4-liter V6, which is fitted in the full-size Toyota Tundra truck and Sequoia SUV, can also be found in the Lexus GX and LX ladder-frame SUVs. Finally, the long-serving naturally aspirated 3.5-liter V6 spent years beneath the hoods of the Toyota Highlander and Sienna, along with the Lexus IS, ES, and RX.

Still, it is worth noting that these engines feature different ECU calibrations depending on the brand and model, resulting in varying outputs. More importantly, Lexus will spoil you in the back seat , but the refinement goes beyond the cabin. The shared engines are wrapped in a nicer package with improved sound insulation, higher-quality materials, and unique suspension setups, elevating the experience for the driver and the occupants.
Besides the shared bits, Lexus gets unique engines for its high-performance and halo models, which are not used in vehicles with Toyota emblems.

The ultimate example is the high-revving naturally aspirated 4.8-liter V10 engine of the discontinued LFA supercar. The mill was developed specifically for this application with the help of Yamaha, and was hand-built in Japan with a "Takumi" expert approach. Each of the 500 LFAs got a V10 that one engineer built and personally approved from start to finish, which helped keep quality consistent across the production run.

Foggy car windows are not only annoying, they can also be hazardous. If it has been one of those mornings and you're already running late, the last thing you want is to sit waiting for the windows to clear. We've all tried wiping it away with our hands, leaving streaks and puddles everywhere, or playing with the air conditioning system without understanding how the window defrost works. While some newer cars have a single button that takes care of it in an instant, there are a few ways to prevent your car windows from fogging up in the first place, from sprays found in stores to vegetables kept in the kitchen.

The quickest way to clear your car's windows is to activate the air conditioner defrost setting, making sure it's set to fresh-air mode, not recirculate. Reducing the amount of moisture in the air helps prevent window fogging, but that is usually easier said than done. Some people even look to common household items like potatoes and toothpaste as DIY solutions, but we'd recommend sticking to more traditional remedies, such as anti-fog sprays you can buy at a store.

Foggy windows are a hassle year-round, but like tire chains and reduced EV range , they're a classic hallmark of winter driving. It all comes down to simple science (no white lab coats required for this one): When hot air touches a cold surface, it cools quickly, turning from a gas to a liquid. This process is known as condensation. Since the air inside the cabin is slightly warmer than the outer surface of glass in winter months, condensation builds up inside. Likewise, blasting the air conditioner during summer makes the cabin cooler, meaning the air outside is warmer, so the outside glass starts to fog.

Think about going outside on a cold, winter morning and breathing out. The hot air expelled from the body hits the cold air and turns to what looks like steam. While less exaggerated, the constant release of water vapor from breath builds up in a car and lands on the glass. Leaving damp clothes or shoes in the back seat can make window fog worse, as can taking a warm cup of coffee into the car on a cool day.

Differences in ambient and cabin temperatures are a key cause of foggy windows, especially when it comes to seasonal extremes, but humidity can also cause this. While a plug-in dehumidifier is the perfect solution in your home, there are a few ways to reduce the humidity in your car to prevent the windows from fogging up. To help control cabin humidity, toss silica gel bags under the seats and in the trunk, and you can swap in all-weather floor mats to keep moisture from soaking into the carpet in the first place.

Controlling cabin humidity stops window fog before it starts, but applying a dedicated anti-fog coating adds an extra layer of defense. While the lore of rubbing a potato on your windshield may seem easy and cost effective, it's temporary and can be messy. Another unorthodox method that actually works is using toothpaste on the windscreen, but this can damage the glass. Plus, anything that leaves residue or streaks can dangerously reduce visibility. We do not recommend these methods. Instead, a safer and more effective way to stop car windows fogging up throughout the year is by using an anti-fog spray with hydrophobic properties — like Rain-X — on glass surfaces. Applying this with a clean microfiber towel leaves a clear, streak-free layer over the glass that stops moisture from turning into fog.

The flex-fuel prototype had various updated components for proper functioning with higher ethanol blends.

For this list, we ranked the SUVs based on their EPA-estimated range, save for one EPA-exempt heavyweight. Also, all listed prices include destination charges. So, let's crunch the numbers and see how this year's electric SUVs compare.

The Equinox EV is quietly making a case as the smartest electric buy for 2027. After the out-of-control price drops for 2026, it now starts at an affordable $36,795. That's slightly less than the base Hyundai Ioniq 5 ($36,900) and only a bit more than the Toyota bZ ($36,575), but the Equinox EV beats both rivals handily when it comes to range.

Even the base single-motor FWD model (220 horsepower) comes with a fairly large 85-kWh battery, which provides a class-leading EPA-estimated range of 319 miles. Meanwhile, the base Ioniq 5 only packs a 63.0-kWh battery and a 168-hp motor, enough for a 245-mile range. The Toyota bZ has an even smaller 57.7-kWh battery that provides an even shorter 236-mile range and a less potent 165-hp front motor. Granted, the Equinox EV's 150-kW peak charging rate can't match the Ioniq 5's, but it keeps up with the Toyota bZ.

Better yet, adding a second motor has a negligible effect on range, with the AWD model rated at an EPA-estimated 307 miles between charges. Choosing the 300-hp AWD model does increase performance quite significantly, though. According to Car and Driver's tests, the FWD Equinox EV needs 7.7 seconds to reach 60, while the AWD cuts that down to 5.8 seconds.

The Equinox EV isn't only good at the numbers game. Inside, it offers enough room for adults in both rows and a useful 26.4-cubic-foot trunk. It also pampers passengers with a smooth ride, and it can even be equipped with GM's Super Cruise hands-free highway driving assistance tech.

The 2027 Kia EV6 ties the Equinox EV with an identical EPA-estimated 319-mile range. However, you'll need at least the Light Long Range trim, which starts at $42,745 and packs an 84-kWh battery alongside a 225-horsepower motor in the rear. The base 167-hp model has a smaller 63.0-kWh battery and an EPA-estimated range of only 237 miles, though it starts at a lower $39,445. Since it shares the 800-volt architecture with the Ioniq 5, the EV6 can use 350-kW chargers, which top up the larger battery from 10% to 80% in less than 18 minutes.

title: Tesla Cybercab's autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn't move
raw_summary: Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely. And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.
summary: Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.
article_paragraphs: Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.
And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps , and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it . Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.
Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X , summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.
Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

raw_title: If The Temerario's Exhaust Note Stopped You Buying One, Lamborghini Has Some Good News Made From Titanium
title: If The Temerario's Exhaust Note Stopped You Buying One, Lamborghini Has Some Good News Made From Titanium
raw_summary: Despite the 10,000-rpm redline and its status as a mid-engined Italian supercar, the Lamborghini Temerario makes a noise that isn't universally loved. Our own Daniel Golson says this car's twin-turbo V8 is one of the best engines he's ever experienced , and Car Throttle says it sounds "incredible." Our own Andy Kalmowitz says it sounds "broken" below 3,000 rpm, while the Throttle House/Grand Tour guys once remarked that unless you're knocking on the redline's door, the Lambo simply "doesn't sound very good." I think the Temerario having to live in the shadow of its naturally aspirated V10 Huracán predecessor has a lot to do with this mixed reception, but either way, Lamborghini has seemingly heard the feedback and is now raising the supercar's aural ceiling by offering a titanium exhaust from Akrapovič as a factory option. The upgrade is very much positioned as a sound enhancement, not necessarily a performance one, because in the first line of its press release, Lambo says it was "developed to amplify the natural acoustic character of its V8 engine while utilizing lightweight engineering."

article_paragraphs: Despite the 10,000-rpm redline and its status as a mid-engined Italian supercar, the Lamborghini Temerario makes a noise that isn't universally loved. I think the Temerario having to live in the shadow of its naturally aspirated V10 Huracán predecessor has a lot to do with this mixed reception, but either way, Lamborghini has seemingly heard the feedback and is now raising the supercar's aural ceiling by offering a titanium exhaust from Akrapovič as a factory option. The upgrade is very much positioned as a sound enhancement, not necessarily a performance one, because in the first line of its press release, Lambo says it was "developed to amplify the natural acoustic character of its V8 engine while utilizing lightweight engineering."

These new optional pipes feature a different geometry and layout, physically wider tubes, custom manifolds, and a tailored silencer architecture. Strategic insulation keeps things cool in hot zones, and NVH was carefully calibrated so specific frequencies are enhanced. Lambo says this gives the Temerario "deep notes" at low rpm and an "incisive acoustic signature" at high ones.

It's made of high-grade titanium alloys, uses precision-cast valve housings, and is hand-assembled "across every component." Lamborghini says it weighs 25.1 pounds, 12% less than the standard exhaust, which means it cuts about 3.4 pounds from the car's curb weight. The tip is black to blend in with the car's rear end, and of course it says Akrapovič on the top so everyone at Cars & Coffee can know you spent the extra dough even when the car is off. There's good news for people who already have Temerarios looking for some extra, better decibels: the part will be available as a retrofit package.

We should note that, before this, the Temerario could already be had with a titanium muffler if you went for the lightweight Alleggerita Package that also bundled in a bunch of carbon-fiber bits, but this Akrapovič system is said to be new and therefore definitely not the same thing. Akrapovič is a Slovenian company that specializes in aftermarket exhausts, and has arguably become the name in the space, a bit like how Brembo is with brakes or Recaro is with seats. Lambo previously worked with Akrapovič on upgraded exhausts for the Urus SUV and Huracán STO .

For reference, the Temerario uses a twin-turbo 4.0-liter V8 along with three electric hybrid motors to produce 907 horsepower. For those who were on the fence about buying one because it apparently doesn't sound quite as nutty as that old V10 (I mean, that's why I haven't pulled the trigger yet), perhaps these new Slovenian pipes will change things for you.

title: I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian's bike
raw_summary: I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg. Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

article_paragraphs: I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.
Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year , it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999 , it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.
Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

article_paragraphs: A cheap pantry staple that can save you a trip to the auto parts store.

There's no shortage of interior car cleaning products available. Whether you're cleaning fabric, leather, Alcantara (faux suede) , glass, plastic, or any other common cabin surface, your local auto parts store will probably have the perfect product for the job. However, as with many household cleaners, you can often replace car cleaners with cheaper, more accessible options you may already have in your pantry. Baking soda is one of the best alternatives.

If your car's seats need a good clean, a baking soda and water mixture is an excellent option. Mix roughly two tablespoons of baking soda with one tablespoon of water, grab a small sponge, toothbrush, or scrubbing brush, and you're good to go. First, spread the baking soda paste on a typical stain and let it sit for 30 seconds to five minutes before scrubbing and rinsing with a damp cloth. If your car has leather seats, skip the scrubbing and check the manufacturer's cleaning recommendations first. For especially deep or large stains, leave the baking soda paste on for up to 30 minutes.

If you're cleaning a larger interior surface, put a tablespoon of baking soda in a small bowl or container and dip a damp sponge or microfiber towel into it. You can then work it gently across most upholstered areas. To be extra careful, it's always worth testing the cleaner in a hidden area to ensure it won't cause discoloration.

Baking soda also absorbs odors well, and in this case, it's even easier to use because you don't need to mix it with water. Just sprinkle the baking soda over the surface and vacuum it up after at least 15 minutes. This method isn't guaranteed to eliminate all odors and may struggle with deep-set smells like cigarette smoke. Nevertheless, baking soda is a cheap, easy option worth trying.

If your car desperately needs a true deep clean that normal household products or interior cleaners can't handle, it could be worth investing in a portable spot cleaner. These cleaners let you spray a dedicated cleaning solution onto an interior surface, scrub it, then vacuum up the dirty moisture. I recently did just this with my Renault's driver's seat, and detailing it required a strong stomach . It was absolutely filthy, and I vacuumed up loads of dirt and grime that had built up over years of use. For everyday spills and smells, though, a box of baking soda is the cheapest place to start.

raw_summary: The Japanese-spec model pairs the standard engine with the heavy-duty TY85 six-speed manual and rev-matching technology.
